documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human resource management (HRM), yet the cognitive and psychological factors associated with human resource (HR) professionals’ intentions to use AI remain incompletely understood. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and appraisal perspectives, this study examines the relative associations of Cognitive Evaluation, AI-Use Anxiety, AI-Related Job Insecurity, organizational AI use across HR functions, and AI Knowledge with behavioral intention to use AI. It also explores whether AI Knowledge moderates these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 285 HR professionals. Confirmatory factor analyses assessed the measurement structure of the study constructs, followed by hierarchical moderated regression analyses examining their unique associations with behavioral intention and the exploratory moderating role of AI Knowledge. Findings Cognitive Evaluation, reflecting perceived usefulness and ease of use, showed the strongest unique association with behavioral intention to use AI. AI-Use Anxiety demonstrated a smaller negative association, whereas AI-Related Job Insecurity, AI Use Across HR Functions, and AI Knowledge did not explain significant unique variance once the competing predictors were considered simultaneously. The comprehensive model explained 66.8% of the variance in behavioral intention. The exploratory interaction analyses provided no clear evidence that AI Knowledge systematically moderated the relationships examined. Practical implications Organizations implementing AI in HR should address both employees’ evaluations of the technology and apprehension surrounding its use. Implementation strategies should demonstrate the practical usefulness and usability of AI through role-specific examples, hands-on training, and opportunities to experiment with AI tools in realistic HR contexts. Organizations should also recognize AI-use anxiety as a distinct potential barrier by providing accessible support, low-risk opportunities for familiarization, and clear communication throughout implementation. These strategies may help create conditions that support employees’ willingness to use AI. Originality/value This study extends research on AI use intentions by examining cognitive, emotional, knowledge-related, and organizational-exposure factors simultaneously rather than in isolation. The findings show that HR professionals’ intentions to use AI are most strongly associated with evaluations of its usefulness and usability, while AI-use anxiety represents a smaller but distinct negative correlate. By distinguishing AI-use anxiety from AI-related job insecurity and individual AI knowledge from organizational AI exposure, the study provides a more differentiated account of the factors associated with HR professionals’ intentions to use AI.

In October 2026, OpenAI released two preprints \cite{openai-brennan,openai-kraetzer}, establishing Brennan's celebrated conjecture~\cite{brennan,brennan2} and disproving Kraetzer's more general $t^2/4$ conjecture \cite{kraetzer, kraetzer-thesis}. While validating these results, we observed that much of their argument is redundant and arrived at a drastically shorter proof of a significantly stronger statement. The goal of this note is to give a short and concise presentation of the reborn proof, sacrificing some of the context and consequences for brevity, and relegating them to a follow-up work. In this particular case the human-AI interaction was fruitful and quite satisfactory, and hoping for a similar future in other subjects, we would paraphrase Rick Blaine: {\em ``AI, we hope this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship.''}

Mainstream point cloud completion methods are unanimously based on deep learning architectures. On one hand, these methods tend to repetitively stacking attention modules to enhance network performance, which drifts away from the neat design of unified and interpret-able networks; on the other hand, nearly all existing architectures rely solely on feed-forward connections to propagate information, neglecting feedback from deeper layers. The recurrent neural architecture, formed by feedforward-feedback loops, have shown its ability to generate Illusory Contours (ICs) in the V1 brain region of mammals; and ICs are essentially a completion mechanism of the brain for visual information. Motivated by this, we design a Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder (BRICE) to "imagine" what is missing in the incomplete 3D point clouds. Building upon the foundation model of Predictive Coding (PC), the plug-and-play nature enables BRICE to be seamlessly integrated into mainstream point cloud completion baselines. Experimental results show that BRICE can enhance various completion baselines on different 3D datasets such as MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom. Our code: Https://github.com/wangyunlei-wyl/BRICE.

In a world increasingly dominated by data, graduates in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) fields are in high demand. This focus often obscures the fact that a significant portion of digital data is social in nature, generated through human–computer interactions. Consequently, experts trained in the social sciences should be equally sought after, yet this is not consistently the case. A contributing factor is the tendency for social and political science departments to adhere to traditional disciplinary boundaries, inadvertently marginalizing their graduates from a growing number of data-centric professions. This paper argues that this gap can and should be addressed. We present a pedagogical project initiated at the University of Bologna, centered on a tailored data literacy and social computing course designed for Political Science students. This study evaluates a dual-case pedagogical investigation evaluating two complementary but empirically independent educational initiatives—conducted across distinct courses, student cohorts, and academic years—unified under an overarching conceptual framework for social science data literacy. This framework combines interactive peer-led learning (Case Study 1) with an instructor-driven, backend Generative AI workflow for multiple-choice question generation utilizing Google Gemini via AI Studio (Case Study 2). Crucially, Generative AI tools were utilized strictly as an offline editorial assistant by the instructor to streamline item creation, maintaining a rigorous human-in-the-loop assessment model, while student examinations remained offline and unassisted. The results and student feedback have been noteworthy, demonstrating improved learning outcomes and high satisfaction, despite methodological limitations including sample size constraints and a quasi-experimental design. We share this experience to encourage colleagues in the social and political sciences to replicate and adapt this model, thereby better equipping their students for the demands of the modern professional landscape.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: The utilization of Artificial Intelligence in developing learning media offers opportunities to present classic literary works in audiovisual formats that align better with the characteristics of digital learning. The aim of this study was to analyze the perceptions of tenth-grade students regarding an AI-assisted animated video of Hikayat Hang Tuah (HHT) as a learning medium for Indonesian language studies. A quantitative approach with a survey design was employed. The study involved 310 tenth-grade high school students in Palembang City. Data were collected using a Likert-scale questionnaire comprising 18 statements across five aspects: visual quality, storytelling, ease of comprehension, learning interest, and perceived benefits. The instrument underwent content validation by three experts (Aiken’s V coefficient: 0.778–1.000) and a reliability test with 30 students (Cronbach’s Alpha coefficient: 0.906). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, with a positive perception threshold set at ≥62.5%. The results indicate that all perception statements fell within the positive range, with scores between 81% and 87%. The highest score was recorded for the statement regarding the visual comfort of the video's colors and illustrations, while the lowest score related to students' willingness to use AI-assisted animated videos in their studies; nevertheless, even the lowest score exceeded the positive perception threshold. Thus, the AI-assisted animated video of HHT was positively received by students and serves as a viable alternative medium for teaching hikayat (traditional Malay tales). These findings reflect student perceptions of the medium and do not demonstrate its experimental effectiveness regarding learning outcomes.

Generative AI is increasingly common in education, but its effect on student learning depends largely on how it is used. This interactive session will introduce practical strategies for creating custom AI chatbots that encourage students to think through problems rather than simply ask for answers. Participants will explore ways to design bots that ask learners to explain their reasoning, consider alternative perspectives, identify assumptions, and revise their thinking before receiving feedback. Examples from healthcare education and other disciplines will show how these tools can support guided inquiry, reflective questioning, clinical reasoning, and decision-making. Participants will review and revise sample chatbot instructions, then begin developing a bot for a course or learning activity of their choice. The session will also cover practical considerations such as choosing reliable source materials, setting appropriate boundaries, protecting student privacy, testing the bot before use, and refining instructions based on its responses. Participants will leave with sample prompts, practical design principles, and a plan for using a custom chatbot in their own educational setting. The goal is to help educators use AI in ways that preserve productive struggle, provide a safe environment for practice, and strengthen students’ ability to explain and defend their decisions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Body mass index (BMI) remains the most widely used parameter for obesity classification and cardiometabolic risk stratification in clinical practice. However, BMI does not adequately reflect body fat distribution or metabolic health, potentially leading to underrecognition of high-risk individuals within the normal BMI range. This study aimed to evaluate the progressive cardiometabolic alterations occurring across the normal BMI spectrum in a large occupational cohort. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 166,008 Spanish workers with normal BMI values (18.5–24.9 kg/m²) undergoing routine occupational health assessments. Participants were stratified into four BMI categories within the normal range. Anthropometric, metabolic, vascular, and lifestyle-related variables were analyzed, including waist circumference, waist-to-height ratio (WtHR), triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, fasting glucose, blood pressure, smoking status, physical activity, and dietary adherence. Logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate the association between BMI categories and adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. Results: A progressive worsening of cardiometabolic parameters was observed across increasing BMI categories despite all participants remaining within the conventional normal-weight range. Individuals in the high-normal BMI category (23.0–24.9 kg/m²) showed significantly higher waist circumference, WtHR, triglycerides, fasting glucose, systolic blood pressure, and diastolic blood pressure, together with lower HDL cholesterol levels (p Conclusions: Cardiometabolic risk increases progressively across the normal BMI spectrum, indicating that normal BMI should not be considered synonymous with metabolic health. Individuals with high-normal BMI values may already exhibit clinically relevant adiposity-related, metabolic, and vascular alterations despite remaining below conventional overweight thresholds. These findings support the incorporation of central adiposity and metabolic markers into routine cardiometabolic risk assessment beyond BMI alone.

Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) frequently coexist and are linked through shared risk factors, haemodynamic stress, inflammation, metabolic abnormalities, and vascular dysfunction. Their combination increases the complexity of stroke prevention, bleeding-risk assessment, heart-failure management, and prediction of renal decline. In arid regions, extreme heat, dehydration, and electrolyte disturbances may add potentially modifiable stressors to this cardiorenal vulnerability. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support integrated risk estimation by combining longitudinal clinical, laboratory, electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and environmental data. Objective: To review current evidence on the bidirectional relationship between AF and CKD, the possible relevance of heat exposure to cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and the opportunities and limitations of AI-based prediction in populations living in arid regions. Methods: This narrative review synthesizes major clinical guidelines and selected peer-reviewed reviews, systematic reviews, and methodological guidance published mainly from 2020 to 2025, alongside key earlier sources. The review focuses on clinically relevant mechanisms, risk assessment, environmental exposures, model development, and research priorities for arid regions. Conclusions: AF and CKD should be managed as interdependent conditions rather than isolated diagnoses. Current evidence supports systematic assessment of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), albuminuria, AF burden, cardiac structure and function, thromboembolic risk, bleeding risk, and treatment-related renal changes. Heat-related physiological stress is biologically plausible and supported by broader cardiovascular and kidney literature, but its specific contribution to combined AF–CKD outcomes in Central Asian arid settings remains insufficiently quantified. AI-based models could integrate these domains, provided they are transparent, externally validated, calibrated, and evaluated for clinical utility and fairness. Keywords: atrial fibrillation; chronic kidney disease; cardiorenal syndrome; heat exposure; arid climate; risk prediction; artificial intelligence; machine learning; Uzbekistan.

This chapter introduces the digital care convoy – a network of family, friends, caregivers, and professionals that helps older adults navigate digitalised health care. Rather than focusing only on the digital health literacy of individuals, this chapter adapts Antonucci’s Convoy Model to show how collective support enables access to and the use of digital health tools. The chapter presents three fluid roles: ‘warm experts,’ who provide empathetic, personalised guidance; ‘co-actors,’ who participate in joint health management activities with older adults; and ‘proxies,’ who operate technologies on behalf of those facing major barriers. Real-life narratives illustrate how these roles shift with changes in health, cognition, and confidence. This chapter discusses ethical tensions regarding proxy use, particularly concerns about autonomy, privacy, and the risk of the older adult’s voice being silenced. It also stresses the difficulties faced by individuals who lack informal networks and argue that the absence of a convoy constitutes relational exclusion, which deepens digital inequality. Looking ahead, we consider how AI agents could become new co-actors or proxies, which raises fresh questions about trust and human agency. Ultimately, we posit that sustainable digital inclusion depends not only on technical training but on cultivating the relational infrastructures that humanise technological engagement.
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: Chapter 1 makes the case that vocation is not only an individual quest but an organisational necessity. Drawing on a wide-ranging professional journey across corporate leadership, entrepreneurship, turnarounds, impact investing and system-building, it argues that organisations, like individuals, lose coherence when they lose sight of why they exist. Through personal narrative and institutional reflection, the chapter shows that purpose is not a decorative ideal but a source of resilience, trust, performance and adaptive capacity. It traces how experiences of crisis, governance failure, cultural transformation and entrepreneurial reinvention revealed a consistent lesson: organisations flourish when purpose is embedded in leadership, relationships, strategy and measurable contribution. The chapter further contends that the age of artificial intelligence makes organisational vocation more urgent than ever. As AI scales cognitive tasks and reshapes decision-making, organisations without a clear moral and strategic compass risk defaulting to efficiency without dignity, optimisation without ethics, and growth without legitimacy. Organisational vocation therefore emerges as a governance imperative: a way to align technology, capital, culture and human agency around meaningful service. The chapter ultimately prepares the ground for applying the Seven-Step Vocating Framework at the organisational level, showing how enterprises can move from passion and vision to coherence, contribution, and measurable impact.

This study examines the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in conjunction with BIM to improve the efficiency of project management in the field of construction projects. There are many issues within the construction industry globally, such as high cost overruns that amount to 80%, and time overruns averaging 20% for megaprojects over $500 million. Although BIM is a very strong tool for collaboration and data management, its capabilities for predicting problems are very limited. In contrast, AI technologies can provide pattern recognition, predictions, and automation, all of which are useful additions to the capabilities provided by BIM. A multiple case study method is applied: Crossrail/Elizabeth Line (UK) using predictive analytics for schedule risk; Google Bay View Campus (USA) using generative design for MEP optimization; and Melbourne Metro Tunnel (Australia) using computer vision for progress and safety monitoring. Findings show documented efficiency gains: 70% faster risk identification (Crossrail), 10-15% MEP cost reduction (Google), and 80-90% faster progress reporting (Melbourne Metro). Cross-case analysis reveals three critical success factors: BIM maturity as a prerequisite, clear problem definition before AI selection, and investment in data quality and change management. The paper concludes with a phased implementation framework for practitioners and recommendations for future research.

As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. This study examines generative marketing, where structured expert labels serve as skill primitives conditioning LLM-generated advertisements. Estimating their causal effects is difficult because outcomes reflect stochastic LLM mediation, high-dimensional label interactions, and multimodal confounding. This study proposes D-VAE (Deconfounder Variational Autoencoder), a counterfactual-inference framework integrating a multi-treatment deconfounder with causal representation learning. D-VAE recovers causally disentangled expert-labeling logic and derives PAC-based bounds on omitted-variable bias from single-treatment confounders. Applied to 29,177 foundation-makeup ad creatives, D-VAE outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. A field experiment shows that recommended configurations increase engagement by 32.7% and perform statistically indistinguishably from human experts, while a simulation study confirms causal attribution under complex confounding and treatment interactions. Overall, the study shifts value assessment from AI-generated products to skills, providing a foundation for pricing and optimizing AI-augmented skill portfolios.

The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) across many application domains has increased the need for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to reduce hallucinations and improve LLM performance. Thus far, several RAG techniques with impressive features and capabilities have been proposed in the literature, making it a herculean task to select the most appropriate RAG techniques for specific problem scenarios. Thus, we propose a conceptual framework comprising main dimensions and sub-dimensions for characterising (defining "what it is") and analysing (defining "how well it does") existing RAG techniques. The conceptual framework was developed through a qualitative analysis of the attributes of RAG techniques reported in the literature. It can serve as a pre-empirical filtering mechanism for researchers and practitioners in selecting the highest-fit RAG candidates that meet specific user and task requirements before empirical benchmarking of RAG techniques, which can be computationally and financially expensive.

Students were surveyed to understand how frequently they use ChatGPT, for what purpose(s), and whether it has helped improve learning outcomes. Thematic analysis revealed three primary themes: (1) Convenience and Accessibility, which highlighted ChatGPT&s;s rapid information retrieval and idea generation capabilities; (2) Perceived Benefits and Limitations, where students acknowledged overall increased efficiencies but expressed misgivings about information accuracy and over-reliance on the model; and (3) Ethical and Cognitive Implications, where conflicting opinions were reported vis-à-vis its influence on academic integrity and critical thinking. Students were asked to complete a survey to find out how often they use ChatGPT, why they use it, and whether they think it improves learning outcomes. Three primary themes emerged from the thematic analysis: (1) Convenience and Accessibility, emphasizing ChatGPT&s;s quick information retrieval and idea generation capabilities; (2) Perceived Benefits and Limitations, where students acknowledged increased efficiency but expressed doubts about information accuracy and over-reliance; and (3) Ethical and Cognitive Implications, expressing conflicting opinions about its influence on academic integrity and critical thinking.

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into higher education has created new opportunities for learning while also raising concerns about accuracy, academic integrity, digital inequality, and overreliance on automated outputs. This study examined awareness, utilization, challenges, and perceived institutional responses to ChatGPT among undergraduate Biology Education students at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. A descriptive survey design was adopted. Eighty questionnaires were distributed to students across 100–400 levels, and 67 usable responses were returned, representing an 83.75% response rate. Data were collected using a researcher-developed Questionnaire on the Extent of Awareness and Usage of ChatGPT (QEAUC), which demonstrated an overall Cronbach’s alpha of .798. Frequency and percentage were used to analyse awareness items, while mean and standard deviation were used for utilization, challenges, and proposed solutions. The findings showed substantial awareness of ChatGPT: respondents demonstrated awareness on seven of eight awareness items, although only 25.4% recognized that ChatGPT uses natural language processing to understand and respond to queries. Overall utilization was high (M = 2.81, SD = 0.81 on a 4-point scale), with particularly high use for content creation, academic research, education, assignments, brainstorming, and conversation practice. Respondents also agreed that important barriers included inadequate internet access (M = 3.64), training costs (M = 3.46), and rote or superficial use (M = 3.51). The strongest proposed solutions were free internet access (M = 3.85), free Wi-Fi (M = 3.82), curriculum integration (M = 3.76), and guided learning activities (M = 3.58). The study concludes that ChatGPT is already embedded in the academic practices of many participating Biology Education students, but effective integration requires AI literacy, reliable digital infrastructure, explicit institutional guidance, and assessment practices that preserve student thinking and academic integrity.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Educational systems throughout the world are experiencing a complete digital transformation which requires schools to abandon traditional teaching methods and adopt digital learning environments that use advanced technology. Cloud computing serves as the main technology which enables this fundamental transformation because it provides users with instant access to expandable computing power through internet-based systems without requiring them to install extensive local systems. The education system underwent a major transformation through the implementation of cloud-based technologies which provided new methods for teaching and learning. Educational institutions and their staff members together with students, use cloud-based platforms to conduct online learning activities and to handle their administrative work while they work together in real time. The research paper presents a complete examination of how cloud computing functions in modern education through e-learning delivery by using a descriptive qualitative research method. The research analyzes data that researchers collected from peer-reviewed journals and government reports and conference papers and institutional white papers which cover the time period from 2010 until 2025. The research study uses academic databases which include IEEE Xplore and ScienceDirect and Google Scholar to obtain key data sources while also using institutional reports from UNESCO and the World Bank as data sources. The research study uses content analysis to extract fundamental themes which include operational cost-effectiveness and data security and then combines them into a unified system that shows how cloud technology determines both contemporary educational results and institutional procedures.The research study shows that cloud computing offers multiple significant advantages to educational systems. The system simplifies access to educational materials through Google Workspace for Education Microsoft 365 Education and Zoom because it eliminates past geographic and infrastructure challenges which restricted student and teacher access to educational materials. The system delivers high cost savings through its pay-as-you-go pricing structure which enables educational institutions to avoid making expensive upfront expenditures required for establishing their own IT systems. Students can work together on documents while taking part in virtual classrooms because cloud platforms enable them to stay connected with their classmates. The system provides essential network expansion capabilities which help educational institutions protect their networks from crashing during periods of high student usage that occur during admission times and final examination periods. Educational institutions can use cloud computing to deploy various educational applications through two delivery methods known as Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) and Software as a Service (SaaS). The applications include Learning Management Systems (LMS) which use MoodleCloud and Blackboard as well as live virtual classrooms and digital libraries that users can search and Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) which include Coursera and edX and advanced analytics and artificial intelligence tools that track learner behavior to create customized learning experiences.The educational sector faces substantial difficulties which prevent it from achieving the complete advantages which cloud computing technology brings to educational institutions. The primary concern centers around protecting data through implementing security measures and maintaining user privacy throughout the process. Cloud systems require advanced technological protection measures to safeguard highly sensitive student information and research materials because they store student grades and personal data. Online learning through cloud platforms requires constant internet access which becomes a major obstacle for students living in rural areas or developing countries with limited internet access. Cloud services create problems for institutions because they become locked into particular vendors which leads to expensive and challenging vendor transitions due to the need for both system compatibility and institutional software compatibility with existing cloud system standards.The research demonstrates that cloud computing functions as a both technology and teaching method which transforms conventional classroom instruction into interactive learning experiences. Cloud technology delivers personalized educational content which matches an individual student’s learning pace while creating equal access opportunities for both students with disabilities and students who learn from distant locations. Cloud computing serves as the essential technological foundation for contemporary education because it functions as an operational IT system which drives future educational approaches and lifelong learning processes in educational institutions. The research study determines that educational institutions need to resolve their data privacy issues and internet connectivity problems and technical expertise gaps before they can fully exploit cloud technology benefits which will lead to the formation of hybrid cloud systems that integrate physical and digital educational spaces.

ABSTRACT Objective Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly transforming artificial intelligence applications, but their unprecedented computational, memory, communication, and data‐management demands pose significant challenges to existing computing infrastructures. Traditional cloud and distributed systems were not designed for the scale, dynamic execution patterns, heterogeneous hardware requirements, and service‐level demands of modern LLM workloads. This paper aims to examine how cloud‐native and distributed systems can evolve to support efficient, scalable, reliable, and sustainable LLM training and inference. Methods We conduct a structured analysis of representative research advances and practical developments in distributed LLM training, inference serving, cloud‐native orchestration, resource management, heterogeneous computing, and edge‐cloud intelligence. We organize the analysis around major system challenges, including computation, distributed execution and system software, resource management and serving, security and privacy, data management, and standardization. We further examine representative resource‐management strategies and emerging paradigms, including serverless inference, federated and decentralized learning, trustworthy distributed AI, and heterogeneous computing with emerging accelerators. Results Our analysis reveals that supporting LLMs at scale requires a transition from general‐purpose cloud infrastructure toward LLM‐aware, cross‐layer, and adaptive systems. Existing approaches have improved distributed execution, elastic resource management, multi‐tenant serving, and hardware utilization, but important gaps remain in cross‐layer coordination, workload‐aware orchestration, data and context management, interoperability, security, and system‐level optimization. Based on these gaps, we develop a research agenda covering future directions in sparse and heterogeneous computation, LLM‐enhanced system software, prompt and context management, autonomous cloud management, decentralized intelligence, edge‐cloud collaboration, personalized LLM services, and emerging computing paradigms. Conclusion Cloud‐native and distributed systems will play a central role in enabling the next generation of LLM services. Future infrastructures should evolve toward more intelligent, elastic, interoperable, secure, and heterogeneous platforms that jointly optimize computation, memory, communication, data, and service objectives. Continued advances in system design, standardization, and cross‐disciplinary collaboration will be essential for realizing scalable and sustainable LLM infrastructures.

Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with knowledge-intensive tasks due to hallucinations and fragmented reasoning over dispersed information. While Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds generation in external sources, existing methods often treat evidence as isolated units, failing to reconstruct the logical chains that connect these dots. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems (CLS), we propose CodaRAG, a framework that evolves retrieval from passive lookup into active associative discovery. CodaRAG operates via a three-stage pipeline: (1) Knowledge Consolidation to unify fragmented extractions into a stable memory substrate; (2) Associative Navigation to traverse the graph via multi-dimensional pathways, including semantic, contextual, and functional dimensions, explicitly recovering dispersed evidence chains; and (3) Interference Elimination to prune hyper-associative noise, ensuring a coherent, high-precision reasoning context. On GraphRAG-Bench, CodaRAG achieves absolute gains of 7–10% in retrieval recall and 3–11% in generation accuracy. These results demonstrate CodaRAG's superior ability to systematically robustify associative evidence retrieval for factual, reasoning, and creative tasks.

Traditional automated code evaluation systems in Computer Science (CS) education predominantly rely on deterministic input-output string matching. While effective for assessing basic execution correctness, classical autograders fail to evaluate code readability, structural logic, algorithmic efficiency, and Big-O asymptotic complexity. Furthermore, students receive cryptic error tracebacks without pedagogical guidance, leading to reduced engagement and persistent anti-patterns. To overcome these constraints, this paper presents CodeGrade, an end-to-end AI-augmented code evaluation and mentoring platform. CodeGrade integrates a Web-based Microsoft Monaco VS Code editing engine, an isolated dual-sandbox execution environment (Judge0 containerized runner), and a Large Language Model (Groq Llama 3.3 70B) into a unified microservices architecture. The platform introduces a multi-dimensional 60/20/20 Grading Matrix that balances functional correctness (60%), AI structural logic quality (20%), and Big-O asymptotic complexity alignment (20%). Additionally, CodeGrade incorporates an AI-powered Socratic Logic Tutor enforcing strict zero-code-leakage constraints, a Monaco Line-by-Line Refactoring Diff Viewer, Web Speech API Text-to-Speech audio reviews, and a Gamified Peer-to-Peer (PvP) Battle Arena. Empirical evaluation demonstrates an average execution latency of 11 ms, high grading consistency (98.4%), and significant improvements in student engagement and code optimization quality.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

This commentary examines the book and offers concluding remarks on healthy ageing and digital healthcare services in the Nordic countries. It identifies three key contributions and future directions. First, the compilation advances nuanced, strength-based representations of older adults’ engagement with digital technologies, challenging deficit-oriented accounts of ageing in a digital world. Second, it highlights the competences required by older care recipients and professionals in digitally mediated care, including domain-specific digital health literacy. Third, it questions assumptions that digital technologies straightforwardly promote independence and autonomy, situating care within wider sociotechnical networks of dependence, support, and responsibility. The commentary calls for holistic, critical, and interdisciplinary approaches to digital health care, attentive to misinformation, data privacy, security, and societal resilience.
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: The generation of fake news on online platforms has grown into a serious problem, compromising public trust, public opinion and the possibility of information-based decision making. In this study, an intelligent Fake News Detection (FND) system to automatically classify news articles as fake or real was developed using techniques of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). A publicly available dataset consisting of 44,856 news articles from the LIAR data set and the Kaggle repository was used, of which 80% was used for training and 20% for testing. The data preprocessing included the following steps: Removing punctuation, Lowercase, Stop-word removal, Tokenization, Stemming, Lemmatization, and TF-IDF (Term Frequency – Inverse Document Frequency) Feature Extraction. The classification algorithms used were Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), Decision Tree (DT), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), which were trained and evaluated with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. Experimental results indicated that SVM outperforms the other models with respect to accuracy (99.21%), precision (99.25%), recall (99.23%), F1-Score (99.24%) and AUC-ROC (99.96%). To make the classifications auditable, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was applied uniformly to all five trained models rather than to the best model alone, permitting a direct comparison of the lexical evidence on which each classifier relies. The attributions converge: four of the five models rank the token “said” as the single most influential feature, and in every case, it shifts the prediction towards REAL, indicating that the models are detecting the attribution conventions of professional reporting rather than topic alone. The results show that the proposed NLP-ML-XAI framework is accurate, interpretable, and reliable for automatic fake news detection, which could be deployed by media organizations, fact checkers, and digital platforms to prevent spreading fake news online.

Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) are one of the most prominent elements of the technological revolution that has been occurring in the defense sector over the past few years. The advent of asymmetric warfare, high-risk operational areas and the requirement for air platforms to operate with low human numbers has fueled the evolution of ground platforms for a variety of mission profiles. This study explores the different types of UGVs developed by countries in recent years based on technical and structural aspects. The mission types, locomotion configurations, power train systems, dimensions, weights, maximum speeds and operational endurance of the vehicles were comparatively evaluated. Platforms of the UGVs that are produced in some countries such as the United States, Germany, China, Russia, Estonia, Ukraine, Serbia and Türkiye were analyzed in this study. The results showed that for small-scale reconnaissance and surveillance vehicles, electric powered, lightweight wheeled systems are the predominant choice while heavy-duty vehicles such as assault and logistics vehicles are mostly hybrid or diesel powered tracked. The use of hybrid propulsion systems has increased due to the need for longer endurance and greater payload capacity for operational requirements. It was also found that there are big differences between the development methods of different countries. Where the United States is interested in platforms that are modular and can be adapted to specific missions, Russia is interested in heavily armed combat systems. China, on the other hand, concentrates on product diversity and cost-effective solutions. Türkiye has made outstanding strides in the development of medium and heavy class UGVs fitted with hybrid propulsion systems, assault and reconnaissance capabilities, and logistics capabilities, since 2018. The study finds that UGVs are progressing from remotely operated systems to artificial intelligence powered, modular, low-signature, multi-mission autonomous systems. Moreover, it is projected that swarm technologies, human–unmanned teaming, artificial intelligence-driven decision-making processes and hybrid energy technologies will be major contributors to the future designs and capabilities of UGVs.

This study compared a 1D-CNN architecture and a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM-Attention model for multiclass electrocardiographic heartbeat classification, incorporating Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques to evaluate the faithfulness and temporal distribution of the evidence used by the models. Experiments used a dataset derived from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, organized into the Normal, Supraventricular, Ventricular, Fusion, and Unclassified classes. The protocol employed five-fold stratified cross-validation exclusively on the training set, epoch selection based on Macro F1 in an internal validation partition, and final evaluation on an untouched holdout test set. The 1D-CNN achieved a test Macro F1 of 0.8681 versus 0.8140 for the CNN-BiLSTM-Attention model, whereas the hybrid model achieved higher Balanced Accuracy, 0.9441 versus 0.9264, indicating higher average class-wise recall. Explainability analysis employed 1D Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, and temporal attention on a class-balanced subset of samples correctly classified by both architectures. Under the adopted perturbation protocol, Integrated Gradients showed positive mean faithfulness gains across all classes for both architectures, whereas Grad-CAM and temporal attention exhibited more class-dependent behavior. Low-to-moderate agreement among the methods indicated that different techniques may emphasize distinct temporal regions for the same correct prediction. Within this experimental setting, the additional complexity of the hybrid model did not translate into uniformly better predictive performance, supporting the complementary evaluation of predictive performance and explainability in ECG classification.

Large language model (LLM)-based creative AI systems tend to produce plausible rather than novel research ideas. This study compares two ways of generating research hypotheses: a genetic algorithm (GA) that recombines Method, Problem, and Goal elements under a fitness function rewarding distance from the literature and literature support for each link, and free proposals by an LLM. Papers and hypotheses share one embedding space built from 2856 arXiv papers. Over 30 runs with budget-matched baselines and outcome measures on held-out and later-published papers, the selected hypotheses were more distant from the unseen literature than unsearched ones, but the GA matched rather than outperformed random search and hill climbing. Across two LLM families, two prompts, and two temperatures, and even when choosing from the GA’s concept vocabulary, LLM-proposed hypotheses were less diverse and closer to existing literature, whereas combinatorial search explored more widely. On 9755 ICLR submissions, the literature-distance novelty measure was practically unrelated to reviewers’ judgments (Spearman ρ ≤ 0.06), so it cannot establish originality. In controlled manuscript generation, LLM judges proved unreliable, and their order-consistent verdicts more often favored manuscripts built on LLM-proposed hypotheses, which blinded human raters tended to rank as least useful. Code and data are openly released.

Amid the restructuring of global value chains (GVCs) and the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution, how firms’ reallocation of human capital relates to escaping value chain lock-in has become a question of growing theoretical and practical importance for China. Traditional static skill-matching theory treats skill mismatch purely as a distortion in resource allocation. In the course of China’s industrial transformation and upgrading, the co-existence of configuration deviation and industrial upgrading is widely observed. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms from 2015 to 2023, this study measures firms’ relative configuration deviations along the compensation and skill dimensions against industry-year benchmarks. Different types of configuration deviation are then identified according to the sign combinations of deviations in these two dimensions. The results show that the overall magnitude of configuration deviation is not significantly associated with firms’ export technological sophistication (ETS). Instead, the direction and combination of deviations matter: firms with a High-high configuration are associated with significantly higher ETS than those in the reverse configuration. Decomposition by dimension shows that the Compensation-premium is significantly and positively associated with ETS but negatively associated with innovation output, whereas Skill-underutilization is positively associated with innovation yet negatively associated with contemporaneous ETS. Channel tests indicate that the High-high configuration is positively associated with two interconnected prospective channels: innovative-talent accumulation and AI orientation. No robust regional heterogeneity is identified in the association between the High-high and ETS. All coefficients of interest are interpreted as conditional associations estimated within a two-way fixed-effects framework, rather than as identified causal effects. Moving beyond the static job–skill matching paradigm, we interpret these findings through a dynamic capability-building lens and discuss sustainability-oriented policy implications for developing countries seeking to design differentiated talent and digital technology policies.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact

documents.abstract: Biodiesel/ethanol blends represent a promising alternative to reduce the consumption of fossil diesel. This work employs frequency-domain dielectric spectroscopy to determine the permittivity of biodiesel/ethanol blends across the full range of compositions, at temperatures between 293 K and 333 K, and within a frequency range from 1 MHz to 30 MHz. Within this interval, the real part of the permittivity is frequency-independent, and electrical losses are negligible. Leveraging these experimental results, a transformer-based deep learning model implementing Tabular Prior-data Fitted Networks (TabPFN) was developed to determine the blend composition from temperature and permittivity measurements. Evaluated via Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation, the proposed TabPFN model predicted the composition with high accuracy, yielding a coefficient of determination of 0.997, an average absolute deviation of 1.0 mol%, and a root mean squared error of 1.6 mol%. These results outperform conventional machine learning algorithms as well as standard analytical inversion models, operating in a single forward pass without requiring hyperparameter tuning or data scaling. Overall, using high-frequency dielectric spectroscopy together with tabular foundation models are the basis of a streamlined, highly efficient strategy for non-destructive biofuel quality verification.

Abstract Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) remain central to the assessment of clinical competence, yet the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into assessment design, delivery, and scoring raises a fundamental question: what evidence of competence are OSCEs intended to generate? This paper argues that AI should be evaluated through the lens of OSCE validity, with particular attention to how it may strengthen or weaken the interpretive chain linking observed performance to assessment decisions. Drawing on Messick’s unitary conception of validity and Kane’s argument-based framework, we examine how AI may introduce distinct threats across the scoring, generalisation, extrapolation, and implication inferences that underpin OSCE interpretation. We argue that generative AI (genAI) creates a particular risk of construct drift, whereby plausible assessment materials or scoring processes gradually reward observable proxies rather than the underlying clinical capabilities they are intended to assess. To translate this validity perspective into practice, we propose a framework that maps AI applications across the OSCE workflow according to their proximity to candidate consequences and the evidential burden required to justify their use. Lower-risk applications, such as design support and post-hoc analytics, may strengthen assessment when accompanied by construct-focused review and human oversight, whereas higher-risk uses, including AI-mediated candidate encounters and automated summative scoring, require substantially stronger validity evidence. We conclude that AI should be adopted according to the principle of concept before capability: assessment communities must first establish what clinical competence means and what evidence should count before deciding where AI has a legitimate role in high-stakes assessment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Digital transformation is a strategic priority across care-intensive service sectors, yet many organisations struggle to realise its intended benefits. Existing research often examines technological, organisational, and environmental barriers separately, offering limited insight into their interconnections within organisational systems. Drawing on Systems Theory and Sociotechnical Systems (STS) Theory, this study investigates digital transformation among small and medium providers within Australia’s National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Using an interpretive qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 participants from 15 distinct NDIS provider organisations in Sydney, Australia, followed by reflexive thematic analysis and systems-oriented interpretation. Participants described recurring associations among technological misalignment, fragmented software, adaptive workarounds, increased administrative demands, and constraints on organisational capacity for digital improvement, with regulatory and resource pressures interacting with these technological and organisational conditions. Building on these cross-sectional patterns, this study develops Recursive Capability Constriction (RCC), a systems-based conceptual framework that proposes how technological misalignment, compensatory adaptation, administrative expansion, and constrained organisational capability for digital improvement may become interconnected through reinforcing relationships. Rather than representing an inevitable or empirically established causal sequence, RCC provides a conditional explanation of how local adaptations may become associated with constraints on subsequent digital improvement. By shifting attention from isolated implementation barriers to interconnected sociotechnical relationships, RCC extends digital transformation research and provides practical guidance for managing digital change in regulated care environments.

Abstract Objective This study asked whether urologists can tell human-written abstracts apart from artificial intelligence (AI)-written abstracts when both describe the same study, and whether the answer depends on which AI model did the writing. Methods Fifteen published urology studies were selected. For each study, the original human-written abstract was paired with three AI-written abstracts covering the same material, produced by Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.5, and Gemini 3 Flash using identical instructions and each model’s ordinary consumer settings. Because all four versions described the same study, the underlying data were held constant, and the versions differed in how that material was written and presented. The resulting 60 abstracts were stripped of identifying information, and eight urologists read all of them without knowing which was which (480 judgments in total). For each abstract, reviewers stated whether they believed it was written by a human or by AI, rated how confident they were in that judgment, and rated the abstract’s quality and credibility on 5-point scales. Results Reviewers correctly identified AI-written abstracts 49.3% of the time, approximately 50%, compared with 62.4% for human-written abstracts ( p = .011). Results depended heavily on which model wrote the text ( p = .003). Abstracts written by Claude were recognized as AI only 40.0% of the time, significantly less often than human abstracts were correctly identified ( p = .003) and less often than GPT abstracts (56.8%, p = .038); Gemini fell between the two at 50.9%. Quality ratings differed only for GPT, which scored lower than human abstracts ( p = .046; omnibus p = .030); credibility ratings did not differ between sources at all ( p = .577). Reviewers who felt confident were no more likely to be correct ( p = .749), and reviewers seldom agreed with one another about which abstracts were AI-written (Fleiss’ κ = −0.009). Conclusion Urologists could not reliably recognize AI-written urology abstracts, and the difficulty came mainly from one model rather than from AI writing in general. How good an abstract appeared had little to do with whether its authorship was correctly identified, and neither reviewer confidence nor agreement between reviewers gave any warning. Reading alone is therefore not a dependable way to detect undisclosed AI authorship.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) policies are increasingly used to make consequential decisions in medicine, finance, education, and public services, yet deploying them responsibly requires knowing not only whether a policy helps on average, but for whom. Existing tools for off-policy evaluation and safe policy learning provide population-level guarantees, but some individuals may experience adverse treatment effects. We recast targeted deployment as a multiple-testing problem: for each candidate unit, test whether the outcome under the AI policy would exceed a user-specified threshold, and control the false discovery rate (FDR) among the selected set. Our method, Conformal Policy Selection, combines weighted conformal $p$-values that account for the distributional shift from behavior to target policy with a two-step selection-and-pruning procedure. We prove finite-sample FDR control and establish a doubly robust asymptotic guarantee, where FDR remains controlled if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correctly specified. Synthetic experiments verify these guarantees across four misspecification regimes, and a semi-synthetic study built on real electronic-health-record covariates illustrates how the same FDR control can act as a deployment safety gate, bounding the harmful treatments that a globally trained policy would otherwise administer to a high-risk subpopulation where it misgeneralizes. The framework offers a principled method for safe AI deployment in high-stakes applications.

Human intelligence has historically produced various solutions to the challenges it has faced thanks to its cognitive abilities such as learning, remembering, comparing, and problem-solving. One of the most fundamental examples of artificial intelligence approaches that emerged by modeling these behaviors specific to intelligence is the artificial neural network (ANN), inspired by the biological nervous system. ANNs, with their similarity to biological nervous systems, present a highly complex system, and with technological advancements, the modeling and applicability of these systems are constantly increasing. In this study, a new ANN architecture inspired by the biological nervous system was designed. To improve the classification performance of the developed architecture, the connections in the network were treated as a binary optimization problem and optimized using the Binary Particle Swarm Optimization (BPSO) algorithm. Following the architecture design, the weights of the connections in the network were optimized using the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) algorithm which works with continuous values. As a result, a network architecture compatible with the biological nervous system, flexible in structure, and highly applicable to various problem types was created. The developed method was tested on Breast Cancer, Hepatitis, Mammographic Mass and Haberman’s Survival datasets. Additionally, proposed model compared with the Genetic Algorithm (GA), one of the most widely used evolutionary computation methods in the literature for connection optimization. Specifically, the proposed model reduces the input layer size from 5 to 2 in the Mammographic Mass domain by applying aggressive feature selection. It successfully reduces computational complexity by eliminating up to 12 hidden neurons in the Hepatitis dataset without sacrificing classification accuracy, thus providing significant structural pruning. Furthermore, it demonstrates high stability across all metrics with minimal standard deviation, proving that the synergy between binary and continuous swarm variants generates highly concise, lightweight, and efficient neural network topologies

The horticultural production model has shown structural weaknesses under current environmental and production conditions. This study aims to analyze the trajectory of construction and expansion of the No-Till Vegetable System (NTVS) in the Metropolitan Region of Porto Alegre (MRPA), Brazil, between 2018 and 2025, based on a qualitative-quantitative action research approach. The process was developed in interaction with family farmers, integrating teaching, research, and extension activities. The results indicate that SPDH is not characterized by the adoption of isolated techniques, but as a gradual process of reorganizing production systems, conditioned by ecological, operational, and structural limitations. Competition with spontaneous plants, nutritional imbalance, and lack of appropriate mechanization were identified as major constraints. Conversely, the participatory development of technologies and the role of sociotechnical networks supported system construction. It is concluded that agroecological transition depends on the articulation between knowledge, material conditions, and social organization.

Background Large language models are increasingly used for informal mental health support, yet their safety during escalating suicide-risk conversations may depend on how prior information is presented. Native multi-turn conversations and reconstructed cumulative prompts differ not only in the presence of prior model responses but also in prompt reconstruction, information concentration, message positioning, explicit integration cues, and conversation-state processing. Objective This study compared suicide-risk recognition, direct safety inquiry, response urgency, and timely real-world intervention across isolated current-turn prompts, reconstructed cumulative user-only prompts, and native continuous multi-turn conversations. Methods We conducted a controlled repeated-measures evaluation of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Doubao using 12 standardized five-turn trajectories: 4 direct suicide-risk trajectories, 4 implicit or internally inconsistent risk trajectories, and 4 non-suicidal high-distress controls. Each trajectory was evaluated under three context-presentation formats. The 24 model-trajectory combinations were treated as matched repeated-measures units nested within 8 independent risk-trajectory blocks. Primary contrasts were estimated using exact trajectory-level sign-flip tests and trajectory-block bootstrap confidence intervals. Turn-level outcomes were analyzed using multilevel mixed-effects models. Exploratory condition-by-model heterogeneity was assessed using a trajectory-blocked exact permutation sensitivity analysis, with a trajectory-clustered interaction model used only as a secondary asymptotic check. Results Timely appropriate intervention occurred in 10/24 isolated current-turn observations (41.7%), 21/24 reconstructed cumulative observations (87.5%), and 12/24 native continuous observations (50.0%). On average across the three systems, reconstructed cumulative presentation exceeded isolated input by 45.8 percentage points (95% trajectory-block bootstrap CI, 25.0 to 66.7; Holm-adjusted exact P = .031), whereas native continuous performance was 37.5 percentage points lower than reconstructed cumulative performance (95% trajectory-block bootstrap CI, −50.0 to −25.0; Holm-adjusted exact P = .031). Exploratory model-specific analyses indicated substantial heterogeneity: the native-versus-reconstructed contrast was largest for Doubao, smaller and statistically imprecise for Gemini, and absent for ChatGPT. Conclusions On average across the three evaluated systems, reconstructed cumulative user-only prompts outperformed native continuous conversations, although exploratory model-specific patterns were heterogeneous. Because the formats also differed in prompt reconstruction, information salience, message positioning, explicit integration instructions, and native conversation-state processing, the contrast cannot isolate the causal effect of prior model responses.

Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support evaluative tasks, raising questions about whether their judgements remain independent when users provide prior evaluative information. This study examined the context sensitivity of GPT-5.5 Instant-generated academic peer-review evaluations under positive and negative user-provided evaluative contexts. Method Sixteen academics evaluated two published manuscripts, classified for the study as relatively higher and lower quality, across four structured conditions. Each participant completed all conditions in separate ChatGPT sessions, yielding 64 peer-review outputs. Descriptive summaries of overall scores and publishability judgements complemented qualitative content analysis. Results Three themes emerged: alignment of evaluative emphasis with user-provided evaluative context, differences in the relative prominence of evaluation criteria, and explicit alignment with the user-provided evaluation. Mean ChatGPT scores were 8.74 and 8.84 under positive evaluative context, compared with 3.37 and 3.64 under negative evaluative context for the lower- and higher-quality manuscripts, respectively. Discussion Because all evaluative inputs included both a verbal evaluation and a numerical rating, the findings reflect sensitivity to the broader evaluative context and do not distinguish the contribution of verbal framing from numerical anchoring. The results highlight a potential limitation in treating ChatGPT-generated evaluations under comparable interaction conditions as independent second opinions and underscore the importance of interaction design in human–AI evaluation workflows.

Overview: Concerns about hate speech and its implications for social cohesion, public discourse, and the safety of targeted communities have been intensified by the rapid expansion of social media, particularly in Iraq owing to its social, cultural, and linguistic diversity, as well as its experience of severe sectarian conflict and communal violence during 2006–2007. Hence, it is important to examine social cohesion and harmful intergroup discourse in contemporary digital environments without assuming a direct causal relationship between past conflict and present-day online hate speech. Gap: Machine learning and Transformer-based hate-speech detection frameworks have significantly advanced in recent times; however, the reliable identification of hate speech in Iraqi social-media discourse remains challenging since online communication in the country often involves dialectal variation, informal and non-standard spelling, code-mixing, sarcasm, implicit and coded expressions, and deliberate linguistic obfuscation. These context-dependent and dialect-sensitive characteristics may not be adequately captured by generic language representations, and classification performance alone may fail to provide enough insight into model explainability, generalization across different forms of Iraqi online discourse, and robustness to linguistic manipulation. Hence, there is a need for a framework that can combine contextual understanding, dialect sensitivity, explainability, and robustness for the Iraqi context. Contributions: A context-aware and explainable hate-speech detection framework has been proposed in this study for deployment across Iraqi social media; the methodology of the proposed framework dynamically combines contextual and dialect-specific information for hate-speech classification by integrating Iraqi-aware text preprocessing, contextual Transformer representations, dialect-sensitive feature learning, and an adaptive fusion mechanism. The system also incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for identifying the linguistic elements contributing to model predictions; robustness analysis evaluates model behavior under realistic linguistic variations and obfuscation strategies. In addition to the computational contribution, an interdisciplinary AI–policy framework is also incorporated, wherein anonymized and aggregated hate-speech patterns can provide empirical evidence for parliamentary and public-policy analysis. The legislative and oversight role of the Iraqi Council of Representatives in addressing online hate speech was also examined in consideration of freedom of expression, privacy, explainability, responsible digital governance, and human oversight. Conclusion: An integrated approach that connects Iraqi-contextualized hate-speech detection with explainable and robust artificial intelligence and parliamentary policy analysis has been proposed in this study, wherein AI is positioned as an empirical research and decision-support instrument rather than a mechanism for automated censorship, punishment, or legal determination. A combination of linguistic adaptation, contextual modeling, explainability, robustness assessment, and aggregated policy-oriented evidence in the proposed methodology provides an experimentally testable and socially responsible foundation for analyzing hate speech in Iraqi social media and supporting evidence-informed parliamentary and public-policy analysis.

topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Large language models increasingly operate in open-ended environments, where they are expected to continually adapt to evolving tasks and distributions, often without access to external supervision. Existing continual learning approaches rely on external supervision, such as labeled data, demonstrations, or reward signals, which can be costly or unavailable in practice. Test-time adaptation removes this dependence by learning from self-generated supervision, but existing methods derive that supervision from the single policy being updated, so once the policy drifts, its own learning signal drifts with it, leading to policy collapse, degraded reasoning, and catastrophic forgetting. In this paper, we propose \textbf{Evolution Strategy Reinforcement Learning (ESRL)}, a continual test-time learning framework that draws its self-generated supervision from a population of policies instead of the single policy being trained. ESRL perturbs an anchor policy in parameter space to form a population of nearby policies, samples one trajectory from each, and aggregates their answers into label-free group-relative learning signals for the central student. The anchor is held fixed within each block and refreshed from the student at block boundaries, so the population stays centered on a stable yet current policy and continues to supply diverse and reliable supervision as the student moves. In single-task test-time adaptation across mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and medical domains, ESRL improves average accuracy by up to 31.7% relative to the base model and 16.6% relative to the strongest test-time adaptation baseline. Notably, ESRL substantially reduces catastrophic forgetting and achieves the strongest final performance in continual learning.

Semaglutide is recommended to be stopped 2 months before planned pregnancy, but maternal-fetal outcomes following continued exposure remain incompletely characterized. We examined 363,778 pregnancies between January 2018 and March 2025 in de-identified electronic health records from a large U.S. federated data network. Of these, 572 pregnancies had a semaglutide prescription within 90 days before the last menstrual period (LMP), after excluding pregnancies involving other glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) therapies, type 1 diabetes, or multiple gestation. Semaglutide was prescribed in 246 of the 572 pregnancies (43.0%) during the first trimester (0 to 13 weeks), in 54 of the 360 pregnancies (15.0%) that reached the second trimester (14 to 27 weeks), and in 45 of the 345 pregnancies (13.0%) that reached the third trimester (28 weeks to delivery). Of the 246 pregnancies with a semaglutide prescription order in the first trimester, large language model (LLM)-curated review of the clinical notes confirmed use in 225 women (91.5%) and use once the pregnancy was known in 186 women (75.6%). Further, among pregnancies with a recorded semaglutide dose, the most common highest dose increased from 0.25–0.5 mg during the 3 months before pregnancy (47.5%) to 1–1.7 mg in the first trimester (46.2%), while the proportion prescribed 2–2.4 mg increased from 18.8% to 23.4%. Among 572 semaglutide users and 101,159 similar pregnancies without GLP-1 use exactly matched on age group, LMP year, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and PCOS, similar rates of pregnancies reached the second trimester (62.9% vs 66.7%; P=0.08), third trimester (60.3% vs 64.1%; P=0.08), and delivery (61.4% vs 65.5%; P=0.06). Among the 572 semaglutide users, 146 women prescribed semaglutide during the first trimester gave birth (“semaglutide-continued”) and 185 women had no semaglutide prescription during pregnancy gave birth (“semaglutide-discontinued”). Comparing these groups did not show any significant differences (q≥0.05) in the risk of preeclampsia/eclampsia, gestational hypertension, new high blood pressure from 20 weeks, gestational diabetes, gallbladder disease, cesarean delivery, or postpartum hemorrhage. Among newborns to the semaglutide-continued versus newborns to the semaglutide-discontinued groups, rates of preterm birth, stillbirth or neonatal death also did not differ. Furthermore, among infants with a recorded 5-minute Apgar score (Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, and Respiration), the mean scores (8.5 versus 8.6) and the rates of scores less than 7 were both indistinguishable between the semaglutide-continued and the semaglutide-discontinued groups. In a secondary comparison of 858 semaglutide-exposed and 3,995 metformin-exposed pregnancies, defined by a prescription from 90 days before the LMP through the first trimester, pregnancy loss or stillbirth did not differ significantly. Among pregnancies that resulted in a delivery, maternal complications, cesarean delivery, preterm birth, and newborn outcomes, including the 5-minute Apgar score, did not differ significantly between the semaglutide-exposed and metformin-exposed groups. Overall, semaglutide prescribing during pregnancy was not associated with significant differences in maternal or newborn outcomes studied in this routine care setting. These observations motivate the need for larger retrospective and prospective studies to rigorously establish the safety of semaglutide exposure during pregnancies with underlying cardiometabolic burden.

Domain ontologies require review against knowledge recorded in evolving external resources. We propose COATER, a method that manages executable review components called arrows. Each arrow compares a scoped part of an ontology with a relevant resource and reports support or challenges to its axioms. Challenges may prompt proposals for completion, correction, or restructuring and become tasks for human or agent-assisted triage. Per-axiom coverage summarizes the assessments. We illustrate COATER with the FSL ontology in software language engineering (SLE): arrows review language coverage, language conceptualization, and software-engineering activities. An LLM-assisted linkage exercise increases compliance with a defined Wikipedia-linkage policy from 405 to 600 of 600 entities. A structured catalogue of SLE resources organizes review opportunities.

This study maps the knowledge structure of AI-enabled climate-smart tourism and examines how artificial intelligence, digital twins, the Internet of Things, remote sensing, predictive analytics, and climate services support adaptation, mitigation, and destination resilience. A systematic evidence-mapping design was combined with controlled bibliometric science mapping. Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR, 77 records were screened, yielding 50 eligible publications available through June 2026. Analyses included concept co-occurrence, temporal overlay, technology–function cross-tabulation, climate-relevance coding, and evidence-maturity assessment. Publication activity increased after 2023, with planning and governance dominating the literature. Only 11 studies explicitly addressed climate risk, adaptation, weather, or resilience, while outcome-level evaluation remained limited. The findings reveal a sensing-to-action gap, as observation, prediction, simulation, implementation, and learning are rarely integrated. The study conceptualizes AI-enabled climate-smart tourism as an outcome-oriented destination capability and proposes a six-stage climate-intelligence cycle connecting sensing, integration, prediction, simulation, decision-making, adaptation, and learning.

Purpose This study develops and empirically validates a Corporate Ethical and Responsible AI (CERAi) lifecycle framework. The framework comprises three interdependent stages: design and development, testing and training, and deployment and usage. The study aims to move the research beyond abstract principles and policy analyses toward empirically grounded, lifecycle-integrated artificial intelligence AI governance theory. It positions ethical AI and responsible AI governance as the two constitutive components of the CERAi construct, and AI trustworthiness as a conceptually and empirically distinct downstream outcome anchored in stage-specific organizational governance mechanisms. The CERAi framework is scoped broadly to encompass governance of both conventional/traditional machine learning models and autonomous AI agents operating within organizational settings. Design/methodology/approach We administered a large-scale survey to 500 attendees at a national AI conference in the United States in early 2026, yielding 143 useable responses from AI professionals across healthcare, financial services, manufacturing, retail and energy sectors.
