We developed and validated multi-item scales for each CERAi lifecycle stage using established ethical AI and AI governance frameworks. Structural equation modeling was employed to assess the measurement model and to test both direct path hypotheses and mediation hypotheses. Findings Both CERAIi design and development and CERAi deployment and usage have significant positive direct effects on AI trustworthiness, whereas CERAi testing and training do not. Our results also indicate a significant serial mediation pathway in which CERAi deployment and usage enhance AI trustworthiness through testing and training, followed by design and development. Conversely, testing and training alone do not mediate the relationship between deployment and usage and AI trustworthiness, indicating that design-stage ethics serve as an intervening (mediating) mechanism through which governance activity enacted at later lifecycle stages is associated with perceived AI trustworthiness. This is consistent with testing and training's association with trustworthiness operating indirectly, mediated by the ethical architecture established during the design and development stage. Originality/value Findings of this study demonstrate that AI trustworthiness reflects differentiated perceived salience across AI lifecycle stages, whereby stakeholders appear to weight visible, deployment-stage governance more heavily than upstream design and testing stage governance in forming trustworthiness judgments, rather than reflecting a definitive validation that governance effects accumulate uniformly across all stages in isolation. This study makes a distinctive contribution by providing empirical evidence for a governance-sequencing mechanism, whereby design-stage ethics function as a mediating pathway shaping the effectiveness of governance activity at later lifecycle stages. To the best of our knowledge, such a mediated, stage-sequential mechanism has not previously been demonstrated using primary data within a comprehensive, three-stage CERAi lifecycle framework linking organizational ethical and responsible governance practices to AI trustworthiness outcomes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to conceptualize corporate social responsibility (CSR) as a potentially need-supportive organizational context. This study examines how CSR-related autonomy, competence and relatedness are associated with employees’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and how these two forms of motivation are subsequently associated with perceived work performance and job engagement among employees of small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, this study analyzed survey data collected from 379 employees working in SMEs in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings CSR-specific competence and relatedness were positively linked to both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Autonomy, by contrast, was positively associated with intrinsic motivation but showed no significant association with extrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation was positively associated with perceived work performance, while both extrinsic motivation and perceived work performance were positively associated with job engagement. Originality/value This study advances employee-centered CSR research in an underexplored emerging-market SME context. This study offers guidance on CSR design choices that prioritize competence development and social connectedness to strengthen employee outcomes.

The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into academic spaces requires a shift from passive restriction to resilient, active pedagogical frameworks. This virtual panel explores actionable strategies to protect academic integrity, promote deep critical thinking, and manage AI use, particularly in foundational courses. Panelists will discuss the implementation of high-engagement classroom interventions. The will offer frameworks for transparent student disclosure practices. Attendees will leave with practical templates for syllabus policies, assignment rubrics, and disclosure benchmarks designed to foster a culture of transparency and process-oriented learning in an AI-permeated landscape.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human behavior. Recent models such as Centaur have advanced this goal by fine-tuning LLMs on trial-by-trial decisions from psychological experiments. However, existing large-scale behavioral datasets do not link the same participants across different tasks, so these models learn population-level regularities but are not trained to model individual-level regularities across tasks. We introduce Cross-Psych-101, a dataset of 591 participants and 261{,}551 valid decisions across 12 Bandit, Tradeoff, Structure, and Social tasks. We train Cross-Centaur to predict a participant's target-task actions from a target-task description and the source-task description paired with the same participant's source-task behavior. Cross-Centaur outperforms off-the-shelf LLMs and Centaur on held-out participants, both within and across tasks. Probing analyses suggest that its hidden states encode participant-level behavioral tendencies that transfer across tasks. These results highlight the potential of cross-task individual-level data for predicting human decision-making with language models. Cross-Pysch-101 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HikaruAsano/cross-psych-101.

The diffusion of generative artificial intelligence is redefining the relationship between older adults and digital technologies. Existing studies have largely explained the digital divide among older adults through traditional digital media such as smartphones and mobile payment, while insufficient attention has been paid to how conversational artificial intelligence changes older adults' entry thresholds, sustained-use motivations, and risk-judgment mechanisms. This study adopts a multimethod qualitative design, with semistructured interviews as the primary method and digital scenario-based tasks as a complementary method. From January to February 2026, the study was conducted in Chedun Town and Xinqiao Town, Songjiang District, Shanghai, with 40 participants aged 60 and above who had internet-use experience and showed a pronounced tendency toward high-frequency smartphone use. The data were analyzed through thematic analysis. Interview transcripts, task-observation records, screenshots of AI conversations, and field notes were triangulated; an initial coding manual, double review, and consensus discussion were used to enhance analytic credibility. The study finds that generative artificial intelligence shifts the technological threshold from procedural operation to need articulation and result evaluation, enabling some older adults to compensate for limitations in traditional interface operation through life experience and language-expression skills. Older adults' sustained use is not driven simply by efficiency, but is closely related to emotional anchoring in later life, experience organization, relationship maintenance, and concrete task handling. Community support, peer learning, and intergenerational assistance constitute important mediating mechanisms through which older adults move from initial experimentation to stable use. Whether older adults truly cross the digital divide depends on whether they can develop the capacities of source verification, contextual delimitation, and boundary judgment. Based on these findings, the study proposes a "conditional crossing" mechanism for older adults' acceptance of AI technologies and argues that age-friendly governance should move beyond interface simplification toward capability enhancement and risk support.
topics: Aging, Elder Care, and Social Issues

documents.abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.

Participation can be defined as a social practice in which every individual, by taking part in public events, builds identity, a sense of ownership and belonging; qualities that are inherently linked to heritage, as it serves as the vessel of a people’s collective memory. Therefore, citizen participation and heritage share attributes that, when combined, could have a positive impact on the management of historic cities. Despite the introduction of legislative changes aimed at making participation more flexible, much remains to be done in practice. Although there are efforts to incorporate the voice of citizens into plans and programmes, it is often the case that the human factor sustaining our historic cities is neither acknowledged in regulations nor allowed to participate actively in urban transformation models. Participation constitutes a complex scenario, but it must begin to be addressed in a real, practical and effective manner, so that all social actors can work together in developing proposals that move beyond the tensions between tradition and modernity, nostalgia and oblivion, ultimately leading to vibrant, diverse, inclusive and sustainable city centres.

Abstract Digital financial service providers often receive more customer complaints than can be examined through intensive review and individualized handling. Prior research has examined technology adoption, service quality, satisfaction, trust, loyalty, and artificial intelligence in finance, but less is known about how complaint records can support transparent prioritization when review capacity is limited. This study develops a customer complaint analytics framework for capacity-constrained digital financial services using public Consumer Financial Protection Bureau records. Because realized churn, customer lifetime value, intervention histories, and treatment effects are unavailable, the empirical target is not customer defection or a proxy constructed from complaint text. Instead, the study predicts an independently observed post-intake service process outcome: whether the company subsequently provides an untimely response. The final analytical sample contains 266,337 complaints received between January 2024 and April 2026. Model development is restricted to 2024–2025 through three blocked temporal validation folds, while January–April 2026 is reserved as an untouched final holdout. Structured attributes, sparse lexical features, and fixed dense semantic embeddings are compared under the same temporal design, with mean development average precision (AP) used for model selection. The selected term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF) logistic model achieves a final holdout area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC AUC) of 0.7653 and AP of 0.04985. Within the highest ranked 10% of complaints, precision is 4.83% against a holdout prevalence of 1.24%, corresponding to a lift of 3.89 and capture of 38.94% of all untimely responses. The study therefore shows that intake time complaint information contains predictive signal available at intake for identifying complaints that later receive untimely company responses and can support capacity-aware early review. These results should not be interpreted as evidence of customer churn, retention effects, consumer harm, or causal service recovery benefit.

This study aims to investigate the significance of cybersecurity awareness, digital literacy, and artificial intelligence in fostering data privacy protection for students and teachers in North India. The study was an exploratory descriptive study with a cross-sectional quantitative design, based on primary data gathered from a structured questionnaire with 620 respondents. The methods used were descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The correlation was positive for all of the variables, and the highest was between the AI-driven cybersecurity and data privacy protection (r = .741, p < .001). The results of the regression showed that artificial intelligence cybersecurity, digital literacy and cyber security awareness had significant predicting power for data privacy protection, accounting for 66.3% of its variance. The results highlight the need for a holistic approach to integrating AI into education, fostering digital literacy, and raising cybersecurity awareness to ensure safer and privacy-conscious learning spaces.

The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms and web-based services has increased the use of user interface techniques designed to influence online decision-making. Among these techniques, dark patterns are deceptive or manipulative design practices that can mislead users, encourage unintended actions, or make it difficult to understand and control their choices. Identifying such patterns manually across different websites is time-consuming and requires considerable awareness of deceptive interface designs. To address this challenge, this project titled “Dark Pattern Finder” presents an intelligent browser-based system that automatically detects and identifies potential dark patterns present in web pages.The proposed system utilizes Artificial Intelligence and machine learning techniques to analyze webpage content and identify suspicious interface patterns. A browser extension collects relevant webpage information, including DOM elements, visible text, user interactions, and other behavioral evidence. The collected information is processed by a backend detection system developed using Python and FastAPI. A machine learning-based classification model analyzes the extracted content and categorizes potential dark patterns such as scarcity and urgency, deceptive messages, forced actions, and other manipulative interface practices. The system also provides confidence scores and supporting evidence to improve the transparency and interpretability of the detection results.To enhance the reliability of detection, the proposed system integrates multiple analysis approaches, including DOM-based analysis, behavioral observation, and state-change information. The detected patterns are presented directly through the browser extension using visual overlays and user-friendly notifications, enabling users to understand potentially manipulative elements while browsing. The system can also associate detected patterns with relevant legal and regulatory information to provide additional awareness regarding potentially deceptive practices.

While Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across complex tasks, they predominantly operate in isolated sessions, lacking the ability to continually learn from historical interactions or adapt to user-specific environments. Existing self-evolution paradigms often indiscriminately inject raw interaction trajectories into memory or skill modules, leading to obscured behavioral patterns and compromised update controllability. Furthermore, as foundational LLM reasoning improves, the bottleneck for agentic evolution shifts from accumulating generic knowledge to effectively managing situational experience. To address this, we propose Darwin-Claw, an environment-adaptive self-evolving framework that systematically distills episodic experiences to drive the comprehensive evolution of operational skills and durable memory. Theoretically grounded in an iterative agent-actor and evolver-critic co-adaptation, Darwin-Claw introduces a Hierarchical Experience Consolidation System that extracts fine-grained error attributions and generalizes them into dynamically updated prototype vectors. This structured situational experience serves as interaction patches for context-sensitive perception and explicit optimization signals for skill refinement. Practically, Darwin-Claw is a readily deployable, automated framework compatible with mainstream agent systems without requiring manual curation. Extensive experiments on WildClawBench demonstrate that Darwin-Claw yields substantial performance improvements, establishing a controllable and stable pathway for the continual, user-centric adaptation of autonomous agents in real-world ecosystems.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to support data analysis and have the potential to make statistical methods more accessible to clinicians and medical researchers with limited programming experience. However, the rapid development of technologies surrounding LLMs has introduced new concepts and workflows that may be unfamiliar to potential users. In particular, tool calling, sandboxing, and data science agents provide different mechanisms through which LLMs can perform statistical analyses, yet the distinctions between these approaches are often unclear. This paper introduces and compares these three developments from the perspective of statistical data analysis. Tool calling allows an LLM to access predefined statistical functions, sandboxing provides a controlled computational environment in which model-generated code can be executed, and data science agents extend these capabilities by combining reasoning, tools, memory, planning, and execution environments to pursue analytical objectives through multi-step workflows. Their application is illustrated using the R programming language together with the ellmer and securer packages. Examples demonstrate how statistical analyses can be performed using predefined functions, code execution within a sandbox, and a simple biostatistics agent. The advantages, limitations, and verification requirements of each approach are discussed, with particular emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and human oversight. This paper aims to provide clinicians, researchers, and statisticians with an accessible introduction to these emerging technologies and their potential role in LLM-assisted data analysis.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted great attention in both academic and industrial communities in recent years. Numerous survey studies have covered various aspects of LLMs, such as learning strategies, applications, alignment, explainability, and evaluation. However, little headway has been made in reviewing data-related aspects for LLMs, despite data being recognized as a key factor contributing to the emergence of the LLMs era. A wide range of data optimization algorithms and techniques are employed in LLMs' training and application processes. These techniques often originate from diverse deep learning domains, with their theoretical inspirations and heuristic motivations appearing unrelated to each other. This study aims to develop a comprehensive framework for LLMs' data optimization techniques to enhance data utilization efficiency. We first discuss data challenges in LLMs' training and inference. Second, we summarize data perception dimensions for evaluating LLMs' data properties. Third, existing optimization techniques are reviewed and categorized into four groups: data selection, augmentation, reweighting, and others. Fourth, we analyze interconnections between these categories. Finally, we identify key challenges and future directions for LLMs' data optimization compared with conventional deep learning approaches.

Background: Brain tumours are among the most challenging neurological disorders due to their diverse histopathological characteristics and overlapping imaging features.Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of brain tumours because of its superior soft-tissue contrast and multiplanar imaging capability.However, accurate tumor classification remains dependent on radiologist expertise and may be subject to interobserver variability.Recent advances in artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, have shown promising results in automated image analysis and tumor classification, with the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making. Aim: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of deep learning applications in the classification of brain tumours on Magnetic Resonance Imaging.Objectives:1. To determine the diagnostic accuracy of a deep learning model for classifying brain tumours on MRI using histopathological diagnosis as the reference standard.2. To compare the diagnostic performance of the deep learning model with radiologist interpretation in the classification of brain tumours on MRI. Materials and Methods:A hospital-based diagnostic accuracy study was conducted in the Department of Radiodiagnosis in collaboration with the Departments of Neurosurgery and Pathology.A total of 30 patients with histopathologically confirmed brain tumours who fulfilled the inclusion and exclusion criteria were included.Preoperative MRI examinations were analysed using a validated deep learning algorithm.The deep learning predictions were compared with histopathological diagnosis, which served as the gold standard, and with conventional radiologist interpretation.Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, overall accuracy, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, area under the curve (AUC), Cohen's kappa coefficient, and McNemar's test.A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results:The mean age of the study participants was 44.8 ± 13.2 years, with a male predominance (56.7%).Glioma was the most common tumor (40.0%), followed by meningioma (26.7%), pituitary adenoma (16.7%), brain metastasis (10.0%), and other tumors (6.6%).The deep learning model correctly classified 27 of the 30 cases.The model demonstrated a sensitivity of 93.3%, specificity of 86.7%, positive predictive value of 87.5%, negative predictive value of 92.9%, and an overall diagnostic accuracy of 90.0%.The area under the ROC curve was 0.94, indicating excellent diagnostic performance.Comparison with histopathology showed no statistically significant difference (McNemar test, p = 0.564).The deep learning model also demonstrated slightly higher sensitivity, specificity, overall accuracy, and agreement with histopathology than conventional radiologist interpretation, although the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.317). Conclusion:Deep learning demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance in the classification of brain tumours on MRI and showed strong agreement with histopathological diagnosis.It performed comparably to conventional radiologist interpretation and may serve as a valuable clinical decision-support tool for improving diagnostic accuracy, reducing observer variability, and facilitating timely treatment planning.Larger multicentre studies with standardized imaging protocols are recommended to further validate these findings before routine clinical implementation.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Mathematical critical thinking in digital learning requires purposeful interaction among pedagogical tasks, digital tools, and students' interpretation and justification of mathematical ideas. This systematic literature review examines the complementary functions of GeoGebra, Problem-Based Learning (PBL), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Meaningful Learning, and Design Thinking. The manuscript reports a qualitative thematic synthesis of 15 primary empirical studies published within the 2020–2026 search period and identified through Scopus, ERIC, Google Scholar, DOAJ, and Garuda. The available reporting record does not preserve complete database-specific retrieval and screening counts or item-level methodological appraisal results; the review therefore does not claim a fully reproducible PRISMA 2020 selection record. Across the cited evidence, GeoGebra provides dynamic mathematical representations; PBL structures problem-centred inquiry; AI offers feedback and alternative approaches that require mathematical verification; and Meaningful Learning emphasizes connections with prior knowledge. Design Thinking is proposed as a learner-centred organizing process through Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, and Test. These differentiated functions support a conceptually coherent, potentially testable instructional pathway rather than a demonstrated effect of the combined intervention. Future research should verify the primary-study corpus, document review procedures in full, and test the proposed relationships in classroom settings.

Instructors need to know whether a student understands a concept, not only whether the student can produce a correct answer, and the two have come apart: a student can paste a physics question into a chatbot and submit a fluent, correct answer without understanding it. We built a conversational AI agent for introductory mechanics that only probes. It is designed as an instrument that a correct answer alone should not pass. Its key measure is cave detection: identifying a correct first idea that the student abandons when a single variable of the scenario is changed. A single right-or-wrong item cannot see this. The agent asks a student to commit to a prediction about an everyday situation, explain it without physics vocabulary, and defend that explanation against a changed case built from the student's own words. It does not teach, hint, confirm, or correct, and it reports nothing until the end. Such an instrument works only if its replies give nothing away. LLM agents tend to leak evaluation: praise, word choice, reply length, and pacing reveal whether an answer was right, and a student who knows stops reasoning. We report design rules that suppress this leakage, derived from eight versions of the agent and more than 40 scripted simulation runs. The obvious fixes often made leakage worse: listing forbidden praise phrases increased praise, and a single worked example in the prompt spread into unrelated conversations. Each changed case had to alter exactly one variable; otherwise a changed answer could not be traced to a single idea. The evidence is simulation evidence only: no real students have used the agent, and the author wrote both the personas and the scoring rules. This paper reports design findings, not learning outcomes.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have made it increasingly possible for individual educators to design and implement their own custom chatbots without advanced programming skills (Abe & Kaneshige, 2025). This workshop introduces practical examples of custom chatbots developed for educational purposes and discusses both their affordances and limitations for classroom use. We would like to share a chatbot creation experience, which we spent one hour building, with a 30-minute presentation. For each chatbot, we will explain its intended purpose, target users, basic specifications, and expected classroom applications. We will also describe the development process, including how the presenters designed the chatbot instructions, refined prompts, and adjusted the chatbot behavior through iterative testing. After introducing these three examples, the workshop will discuss the potential benefits of custom chatbots. In particular, we will show how they can help users access relevant information more efficiently, provide more focused guidance than general-purpose AI tools, and support educators who want to create AI-assisted learning environments tailored to specific instructional goals. The workshop will critically examine current limitations. Even after repeated tuning, custom chatbots may still produce inaccurate, incomplete, or contextually inappropriate responses. Therefore, developers and educators remain responsible for checking the accuracy of the content and deciding whether the chatbot output is appropriate for learners. By combining demonstration, reflection, and critical discussion, this workshop aims to help participants understand how custom chatbots can be used responsibly and realistically in educational settings.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Enterprise data assistants using large language models (LLMs) promise democratized data access in organizations. Yet in our real-world deployment within the CFO unit's data lake at an industry partner, we observed that business users frequently pose imperfect prompts that include domain-specific vocabulary and lack schema references or structural information. This Design Science Research study examines automatic resolution using a semantic mediation layer. We design and evaluate two design variants: schema-based mediation via semantic similarity, and knowledge graph-based mediation leveraging an automatically constructed knowledge graph from the data lake. Our simulation-based evaluation using real-world data, supported by LLM-as-a-Judge assessments and human validation, shows that knowledge graph-based mediation outperforms the schema-based approach in Precision, Recall, F1, and preserving user intent. We propose a design principle for knowledge graph-based mediation, demonstrating that structured knowledge representation bridges user intent and database structure and guides the design of enterprise data assistants across skill levels.

Artificial intelligence (AI) for Science is often described as a progression from human-directed assistance toward increasingly autonomous AI scientists. Human-AI collaboration offers a further mode in which human and AI contributions substantively shape scientific reasoning, judgments, and the course of inquiry. Existing research addresses work allocation, human-AI coordination, and system evaluation, but how these aspects interact to shape collaborative scientific systems remains insufficiently articulated. We develop the 9A Framework for Human-AI Collaborative Science (HACS) to connect these considerations across three layers. The organization layer specifies what scientific activities are required (Activity), who performs them (Actor), and who holds authority over consequential decisions (Authority). The coordination layer addresses how participants access relevant research information (Awareness), how scientific work advances through iterative proposal, execution, examination, revision, and resolution (Accountability), and when collaborative arrangements should be adjusted (Adaptability). The evaluation layer establishes what constitutes effective system performance (Achievement), how comparisons can be designed to identify the effects of organizational and coordination choices (Attribution), and what evidence supports the resulting conclusions (Assurance). Together, these layers frame HACS as a system-design problem, providing a basis for designing collaborative scientific workflows and for empirically comparing their effectiveness.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to design instructional materials in higher education, yet limited evidence exists on students’ perceptions of the cognitive demands and learner-related competencies involved. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, this study examined university students’ perceptions of GenAI-supported instructional material design according to gender, age, and admission grade. A quantitative, non-experimental, ex post facto study was conducted with 451 university students enrolled in education-related undergraduate and master’s programmes. The instrument assessed perceived usefulness, beliefs concerning metacognitive practices, prior knowledge, and problem-solving strategies, and perceived intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Participants generally reported positive perceptions. Female students reported significantly higher scores on the metacognitive skills, prior knowledge, and problem-solving skills dimensions, although effect sizes were small. These differences should be interpreted cautiously, given that female students represented 82% of the sample. No statistically significant gender differences were detected in the cognitive load dimensions. Age showed only a weak negative association with extraneous cognitive load, whereas admission grade was positively associated with metacognitive scores in both gender groups and with prior knowledge and problem-solving scores among female students. The findings describe students’ beliefs about the practices and cognitive demands associated with GenAI-supported material design and may inform training in the critical review and pedagogical adaptation of AI-generated teaching materials.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The growing presence of AI in higher education has prompted instructors to move beyond passive adoption, to deliberate theory-grounded design. This session presents two custom AI chatbots (DisneyBot and Rico) developed within a teacher preparation course as the technology-enhanced component of a multidisciplinary instructional unit. DisneyBot is built on the ChatGPT platform to guide learners through an exploration of Disney parks, and Rico, is built on the Gemini platform as an interactive guide to information about Puerto Rico by scaffolding learning across four subject-specific lesson modules – Social Studies, ELA/ENL, Science, and Spanish. Both chatbots were developed to support differentiated and interactive learning for 4th and 5th grade students through a virtual field trip framework, with the broader goal of connecting classroom content to authentic real-world experiences. The design of each chatbot was grounded in UDL principles (CAST, 2018). Rather than serving as static information repositories, the chatbots were intentionally designed to function as interactive instructional mediators which use prompting inquiry, guiding subject-specific exploration, and offering differentiated entry points for learners with varying needs and language backgrounds (Vygotsky, 1978). The differences between the two platforms, in terms of interface architecture, customization depth, persona design, and interaction affordances, form the basis of a comparative analysis that will anchor the session. Participants will interact directly with both chatbots, examine the instructional design decisions behind them, and leave with a working framework for developing purpose-built AI chatbots that can be tailored to their own teaching contexts and disciplines.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Trade-based money laundering (TBML) hides in the documents of trade rather than in the payments that settle it. Conventional transaction-monitoring systems examine amounts, frequencies, and velocities, and are therefore blind to the documentary substance of a shipment; machine-learning systems trained on transaction-level features inherit the same blindness; and static models of either kind decay as laundering typologies migrate across goods, corridors, and forgery techniques. This paper describes a detection system, disclosed in U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 64/170,275, that is organised around the documents themselves. Heterogeneous trade documents — commercial invoices, bills of lading, customs declarations, packing lists, letters of credit, and associated payment records — are parsed into canonical shipment assertions that retain provenance metadata, and entity mentions across documents are resolved to canonical identities, with alias collisions preserved as signals rather than merged away. The resolved material is assembled into a heterogeneous entity–document–shipment graph whose edges are of two kinds: documentary edges recording what each document declares, and consistency edges — computationally verifiable assertions linking attributes across documents that purport to describe the same shipment — each carrying a consistency score. From this graph the system computes features that encode known TBML typologies at the documentary level: unit-price deviation against benchmark price distributions indexed by HS code, trade corridor, and time window; cross-document quantity and value reconciliation; circular-trading cycles; phantom-shipment document asymmetries; and shipment-structuring patterns. A calibrated scoring model emits per-shipment and per-entity risk scores with machine-readable documentary reason codes, exposed through a real-time scoring API designed for pre-settlement interception. Investigation outcomes — suspicious activity report filings, confirmed typologies, and analyst labels — close the loop: confirmed activity reweights the suspicious-entity subgraph and re-runs community detection, labelled cases retrain the model, an active-learning strategy allocates analyst review by uncertainty over graph neighbourhoods, and per-corridor stationarity testing of benchmark price distributions detects typology drift and triggers benchmark re-estimation, targeted labelling, and model refresh — all without manual feature re-engineering. A further embodiment extends the graph across the full lifecycle of direct-to-consumer cross-border e-commerce. The paper reports no evaluation and no measurements; numerical values cited are the design targets and structural parameters stated in the disclosure.

Debate and argumentation exercises are widely used in higher education and professional training to develop critical thinking, yet their outcomes are often assessed with general, subjective criteria. This study aims to develop and validate an analytic rubric that integrates three constructs—evidence quality, logical soundness, and cognitive engagement—for evaluating performance in debate and argumentation-based training. An integrative design was employed, comprising theoretical analysis of existing evaluation systems, construct and descriptor development, expert review by five specialists in education and logic, and a pilot study in which two independent raters assessed 30 university students during a debate exercise. The final rubric comprises three constructs and nine criteria, each with level-specific descriptors. Experts rated its content completeness, precision, and applicability highly (mean 4.6 on a 5-point scale). The pilot study showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.85) and substantial inter-rater agreement, confirming the rubric’s reliability and objectivity; the comparatively lower scores on logical soundness indicate a priority area for instruction. The rubric functions not only as an assessment instrument but also as a diagnostic and formative tool that clarifies expectations for learners and guides instructors in planning debate-based teaching. Rater training and further adaptation to different age groups, debate formats, and AI-assisted assessment are recommended.

This study developed and evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)-integrated digital learning modules for Food and Beverage Operations under the Strengthened Senior High School Tech-Pro Curriculum. Using a developmental-descriptive research design with a one-group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental component, it involved 84 Grade 11 learners and five TLE/TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Agusan del Sur, together with three expert validators. The modules were examined in terms of instructional features, competency alignment, validity, and acceptability. Expert evaluation questionnaires, teacher and student acceptability questionnaires, and achievement tests supplied the data, which were analyzed using means, standard deviations, mean percentage scores, independent-samples t-tests, and a paired-samples t-test. The six instructional feature dimensions were rated highly evident (means = 4.60–4.80), and the five validity dimensions were assessed as highly valid (means = 4.67–4.80). Teachers and students considered the modules highly acceptable, with no statistically significant differences in their ratings across the five dimensions (all p > .05). The reported mean percentage score rose from 69.4 on the pretest to 78.0 on the posttest. The paired comparison of achievement-test scores was statistically significant (t = −11.303, p < .001). The findings support the modules’ suitability as supplementary, competency-aligned learning resources, while the one-group design limits causal interpretation. Continued refinement, responsible AI-use guidance, and testing in additional instructional settings are recommended.

In-depth knowledge of geometric design principles is a prerequisite for delivering road projects that provide safe and efficient multimodal mobility for all users. Historically, Kentucky Transportation Cabinet (KYTC) early-career design staff arrived at the agency with little design experience. The agency has relied on a combination of short courses and mentorship provided by experienced personnel to bring early-career design staff up to speed on design best practices. However, this approach to training carries limitations. Employee turnover and imposing workloads make it challenging for early- and even mid-career design professionals to receive guidance from seasoned designers who have long tenures at KYTC. And it hinders efforts to implement a consistent design philosophy across the agency. Recognizing that young designers, as well as project managers and project reviewers, would benefit from a course focused on geometric design, Kentucky Transportation Center (KTC) researchers worked with Cabinet staff to develop and deliver the Roadway Geometry Fundamentals Course. This five-day training introduces participants to a mix of foundational concepts (e.g., horizontal and vertical alignment, sight distance, cross-sectional elements, speed management, intersection design, roadside safety) and advanced topics (e.g., innovative design, context classification, human factors). The course blends instructor-led lectures, group exercises, and discussion to achieve learning objectives. A pilot version of the course was delivered in October 2025, and multiple offerings are planned for 2026. Long term, KYTC views the Roadway Geometry Fundamentals Course as an important vehicle for achieving agencywide consistency in design practice and elevating Kentucky to a position of national leadership in innovative design and road safety.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Healthcare waste management directly impacts patient safety, occupational health, and healthcare quality. Despite regulatory frameworks, healthcare institutions frequently encounter operational barriers due to unstandardized practices, insufficient continuous training, and limited managerial diagnostic tools. This study aimed to develop, content-validate, and pilot-test the Healthcare Waste Management Assessment Instrument (IAGRAS) as a decision-support tool for hospital governance and quality improvement. A mixed-methods study was conducted at a tertiary-level accredited hospital in Brazil. IAGRAS was structured around seven key performance indicators using an ipsative scoring system adapted from the Competing Values Framework. Content validity was evaluated by an expert panel using the Content Validity Index (CVI). A pilot application was performed with 50 nursing and hygiene professionals. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the D'Agostino test, Coefficient of Variation, and sector-specific performance mapping using BioEstat 5.0. Expert evaluation confirmed 100% agreement, yielding a CVI of 1 across all seven indicators. Pilot data demonstrated normal distribution (p>0.05). The overall performance mean reached 36% for the 'High Degree' knowledge category. Significant sector variations were identified: the Surgical Center (50%) and Hygiene/Cleaning department (43%) achieved the highest compliance scores, whereas the 4th-floor (26%) and 5th-floor (27%) surgical wards revealed major knowledge gaps regarding waste management plans, transport logistics, and regulatory standards. High Coefficients of Variation (up to 79.7%) highlighted substantial perceptual heterogeneity among staff. IAGRAS proved to be a content-valid and feasible diagnostic instrument for identifying operational bottlenecks and guiding targeted educational and administrative interventions in hospital settings. Its integration into routine institutional audits can strengthen hospital governance, biosafety culture, and care quality.

Background: Prostate cancer is one of the leading malignancies among men worldwide.Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI) has become an essential imaging modality for the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer.Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have shown promising potential in improving the accuracy and consistency of prostate MRI interpretation.Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence-assisted multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging for the detection of clinically significant prostate cancer.Materials and Methods: A hospital-based prospective diagnostic accuracy study was conducted among 50 male patients with clinical suspicion of prostate cancer.All participants underwent AI-assisted multiparametric MRI of the prostate, including T2-weighted imaging, diffusion-weighted imaging, apparent diffusion coefficient mapping, and dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging where indicated.MRI findings were interpreted using AI-assisted software, and all patients subsequently underwent prostate biopsy.Histopathological examination served as the reference standard.Diagnostic performance was assessed by calculating sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), diagnostic accuracy, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.Results: The mean age of the participants was 66.2 ± 7.8 years.Histopathology confirmed clinically significant prostate cancer in 34 (68%) patients.AI-assisted mpMRI correctly identified 31 true-positive and 12 true-negative cases, with 4 false-positive and 3 false-negative results.The sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and overall diagnostic accuracy were 91.2%, 75.0%, 88.6%, 80.0%, and 86.0%, respectively.The area under the ROC curve was 0.89, indicating excellent diagnostic performance.A statistically significant association was observed between AI-assisted mpMRI findings and histopathological diagnosis (Chi-square test, p < 0.001).Conclusion: Artificial intelligence-assisted multiparametric MRI demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy for detecting clinically significant prostate cancer and showed excellent agreement with histopathological findings.AI can serve as an effective decision-support tool for radiologists by improving lesion detection, reducing interobserver variability, and facilitating appropriate patient selection for biopsy.Larger multicentre studies are required to further validate these findings before widespread clinical implementation.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: Problem Definition: For 433,000 patients in the United States with advanced kidney failure, hemodialysis is a life-sustaining treatment. Approximately 7,600 outpatient dialysis clinics serve these patients, whose treatments cost over $25 billion annually. Each treatment involves a pre-treatment “put-on” task and a post-treatment “take-off” task performed by patient care technicians (PCTs). These frontline workers face intense, overlapping demands that can compromise patient safety and contribute to PCT burnout. We study how to jointly schedule PCTs and patients to reduce makespan and increase labor efficiency in dialysis clinic operations through better patient flow. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-ons as soon as a technician and station are free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons and the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. We derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s makespan under constant treatment durations and show that interlaced schedules achieve the shortest completion time, whereas tandem configurations can reduce labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations and stochastic task times and arrivals to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to the primary driver of labor efficiency: minimizing the time that stations sit unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies of the push approach for a single pod, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system while increasing the standard time allotted for tasks can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks. Methodology/Results: We first analyze the prevailing “push” approach, which starts put-on tasks for treatment as soon as a station is free. We then propose two alternatives: an “interlaced” scheme that staggers put-ons and take-offs to reduce idle time, and a “tandem” scheme that pairs two PCTs — one specializing in put-ons, the other in take-offs — across twice as many stations. Under standard conditions, we derive closed-form expressions for each approach’s completion time and show that interlacing finishes earliest with homogeneous treatment durations, while tandem configurations can lower labor per patient. We also incorporate heterogeneous treatment durations to show numerically that our insights are robust. Managerial Implications: In contrast to the push-focused approach, these insights direct facility administrators’ attention to what is most important for labor efficiency: minimizing the time that a station is unoccupied between successive patients. Due to the inefficiencies associated with the push approach, transitioning to an interlaced or tandem system with increased standard task times can alleviate workplace stress and promote patient safety without increasing labor costs. Specifically, dialysis clinic managers could move from the common 15/15-minute put-on/take-off scheduling standard to a 25/20-minute standard, thereby allotting PCTs 50% more time to complete tasks.

This article examines the didactic possibilities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the organization of mother tongue lessons, their role in the educational process, and their influence on the development of students' knowledge. It analyzes the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence tools for taking individual learning needs into account, differentiating language-related tasks, developing written and oral communication skills, and assessing learning. It also addresses pedagogical appropriateness, the reliability of information, and the need to maintain teacher oversight when introducing these technologies into mother tongue education. The article substantiates that the effective use of artificial intelligence can increase students' interest in language learning and help accommodate individual differences in the learning process.

Smart city policies often equate investment in digital infrastructure with sustainable urban change, thus assuming that infrastructure is simply a technical layer devoid of institutional and societal context. This study uses qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA Pro version 2024 and focuses on the “Digital Infrastructure Ecosystem” as it appears in strategic plans of Konya city (Turkiye) and Bucharest Sector 5 (Romania). The coding was performed by two independent researchers who achieved a Cohen’s Kappa of .89. The analysis reveals striking differences between the two cities in the three categories of Connectivity and Hardware, Data Security and Management, and System Integration, as Konya employs a hardware-centric development based on fiber-optic backbone, radio connections, and server infrastructure, while Bucharest seeks to migrate from installation of cables to the provision of services (public Wi-Fi, super-app). The results are assessed through the Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Vial’s digital transformation theory (2019), platform ecosystem approach, and dynamic capabilities theory, thus concluding that infrastructural investment itself is of no transformational value without institutional learning capacity and multi-actor governance mechanisms. By highlighting the conflict between “global compliance” and “local context” in the development of smart cities, the study provides a comparative and interdisciplinary contribution.
topics: Innovative Approaches in Technology and Social Development

documents.abstract: Digital self-management is increasingly used to support people with chronic non-communicable diseases between visits, but its public health value depends on integration into routine care. This SANRA-informed critical narrative mini review synthesized 28 sources identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, backward citation tracking and targeted supplementary searches. It examines digital self-management as service redesign across three delivery models: patient centered digital support, remote patient monitoring, and integrated primary care or community coordination. It also analyzes three implementation tensions: empowerment versus digital exclusion, data visibility versus clinical accountability, and engagement versus uncertain long term outcomes and workload. Evidence suggests benefits for engagement, behavioral support and selected intermediate indicators, but these benefits remain uneven. Public health implementation should therefore prioritize accountable workflows, interoperable procurement, equity oriented support, safe use of large language model based agents, and evaluation of outcomes, safety, equity, cost and workforce burden. Digital self-management should be judged by whether it supports routine, inclusive and sustainable chronic disease care.

Digital technologies are becoming increasingly embedded in undergraduate dental curricula, with the potential to support learning and skills development. This scoping review mapped recent evidence on the implementation and educational applications of contemporary digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify studies published between 2021 and 2025. The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines and included studies investigating digital technologies in undergraduate dental education. A total of 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. The identified technologies included virtual reality and simulation-based learning systems, digital and 3D-printed educational models, digital assessment and feedback systems, web-based learning platforms, artificial intelligence applications, CAD/CAM technologies, and digital clinical devices. Across the included studies, the reported educational outcomes most commonly concerned practical performance, knowledge acquisition, student engagement, self-assessment, and satisfaction, with many studies focusing on short-term preclinical or learner-reported outcomes. Virtual simulation and digital assessment systems were the most extensively investigated technologies. The available evidence suggests that digital technologies may support undergraduate dental education when used as adjuncts to conventional teaching methods. However, the effectiveness of specific blended-learning models requires direct comparative evaluation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal and methodologically rigorous studies examining long-term knowledge retention, clinical competence, educational quality, and the transfer of acquired skills to professional practice.

Organic agriculture is growing rapidly in India, yet organic supply chains remain structurally fragmented, particularly in smallholder-dominated regions such as South Tamil Nadu. Digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising solutions to persistent challenges, including inadequate cold-chain infrastructure, limited traceability, intermediary-dependent marketing and certification workflow inefficiencies. This systematic review draws on evidence from 30 peer-reviewed and institutional publications. These sources were identified through a PRISMA-compliant search of Scopus, Elsevier, Taylor & Francis, Web of Science, IEEE, MDPI, Wiley, FAO, and government databases. The findings indicate that AI-enabled precision farming, machine learning-based demand forecasting, Internet of Things-enabled cold-chain monitoring, and blockchain-supported traceability improve production efficiency, market access and organic supply chain transparency. However, widespread adoption is constrained by inadequate rural connectivity, limited digital literacy, incompatibility between digital platforms and Participatory Guarantee System certification workflows, and weak first-mile infrastructure. This review proposes the Digital Transformation and AI Readiness Framework for Organic Supply Chains (DARF-OSC). DARF-OSC is a five-stage conceptual model that integrates Diffusion of Innovations theory with the Resource-Based View. Also, this review identifies five key research gaps and tiered policy recommendations for South Tamil Nadu.
topics: Digitalization and Economic Development in Agriculture

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the intersection of digital technology and cultural heritage education, focusing on the fundamental tension between technological innovation and authentic cultural engagement. Through analysis of virtual reality applications, digital storytelling, and multimedia platforms in educational contexts, this chapter explores how digital tools simultaneously expand access to cultural resources while potentially distancing students from embodied cultural experiences. The accessibility-authenticity paradox emerges as a central challenge, alongside concerns about superficial engagement and the speed of digital information consumption. This chapter proposes pedagogical frameworks for conscious technology integration, emphasizing hybrid approaches that strategically combine digital and physical cultural encounters. Recommendations address educator preparation, institutional policies, and the development of critical digital cultural literacy among students. The chapter concludes by examining emerging technologies including artificial intelligence and metaverse environments, identifying research gaps, and advocating for theoretical frameworks that balance innovation with cultural integrity in heritage education.

Food microbiology is moving from episodic, laboratory-centered testing toward connected systems that can detect, interpret, and anticipate microbial hazards across food production and distribution. This transition is being driven by the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), biosensors, computer vision, spectroscopy, predictive microbiology, Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructure, and digital-twin concepts. The value of these technologies lies not in replacing reference microbiological methods, but in shortening the interval between sampling, evidence generation, risk interpretation, and corrective action. AI can extract patterns from images, spectral fingerprints, sensor signals, molecular data, and environmental measurements; biosensors can convert biological recognition into rapidly measurable signals; and connected monitoring architectures can place these outputs within dynamic process and supply-chain contexts. Recent studies demonstrate progress in deep-learning-based microbial identification, machine-learning-assisted biosensing, non-destructive hyperspectral and volatile sensing, smartphone-enabled field analysis, and predictive models that integrate temperature, pH, water activity, and other determinants of microbial behavior. However, translation from proof-of-concept studies to routine food control remains constrained by matrix effects, limited external validation, data drift, small or unrepresentative datasets, inconsistent reporting, device interoperability, cybersecurity, and uncertain regulatory pathways. This chapter examines the principal components of digital food microbiology, emphasizes their integration into practical food-safety workflows, and proposes a validation-oriented perspective for responsible deployment. The emerging paradigm is therefore best understood as augmented microbiology: conventional culture and molecular reference methods remain essential, while digital tools add speed, continuity, predictive capacity, and decision support.

Background. In the context of healthcare digital transformation, telemedicine (TM) and artificial intelligence (AI) are being integrated into clinical practice; however, the pace of their implementation outpaces the analysis of their impact on workflows, workload, and physicians’ psychological acceptance. Studying systemic barriers and the human factor is essential for the successful scaling of digital tools in primary care. Objective: to assess real-world experience, identify key barriers, and determine the relationship between physicians’ expectations and practical challenges of implementing TM and AI in the activities of outpatient medical professionals. Materials and methods. A cross-sectional study was conducted using an anonymous online survey of 897 medical professionals from outpatient clinics in the Moscow region. The questionnaire covered socio-demographic and professional characteristics, frequency and formats of TM, AI and EHR use, as well as perceived barriers and risks. Statistical analysis employed descriptive statistics and Pearson’s χ² test (p < 0.05). Results. Daily TM consultations are conducted by 49.7% of physicians, predominantly in audio format (46.5%). Despite recognizing TM effectiveness for chronic patient follow-up (63.3%), 30.6% report increased workload, and 38.3% consider no more than two consultations per day optimal. The main TM barriers are technical failures (29.3%) and low patient digital literacy (16.2%). Regarding AI, a gap was revealed: readiness for use is 55%, while 60.5% have no practical experience; 50.1% fear degradation of their diagnostic skills. Major systemic issues include insufficient interoperability (43.6%) and lack of training (22.8%). Statistical analysis confirmed significant associations between AI use and expectations (p < 0.05), and between training needs and AI readiness (χ² = 23.979; p < 0.001). Conclusion. A persistent gap was identified between positive perceptions of digital technologies’ potential and the real challenges of their integration. The barriers – technical, organizational, and psychological – are systemic and require comprehensive solutions: specialized training, minimization of technical failures, ensuring information systems interoperability, and revision of workload standards considering the time spent on TM consultations.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose This scoping review maps and synthesises fragmented research on disability inclusion from a workplace culture perspective and develops a definition of a disability inclusive workplace culture. Design/methodology/approach Following Arksey and O'Malley's scoping review framework, 32 empirical studies across organisational settings were systematically reviewed. The studies were charted according to their characteristics and analysed thematically. The analysis was then synthesised into a definition capturing how disability inclusive workplace cultures are constituted. Findings The review finds that disability inclusive workplace cultures comprise shared patterns of organisational structures, social practices and psychological experiences that enable employees with disabilities to access and engage meaningfully in the cultural life of the organisation. Cultural inclusion develops through the complex interaction of these dimensions, with leadership and job design acting as central mechanisms. Such cultures are characterised by diversity practices and inclusive leadership, by supportive peer relations and inclusive norms and by employees' experiences of self-confidence, belonging and fairness. In this way, a disability inclusive workplace culture represents a structural framework, a social practice and a subjective experience. Originality/value This review is the first to provide an empirically grounded definition of a disability inclusive workplace culture. The review contributes to the field of disability studies in organisations by conceptualising inclusion as a cultural phenomenon and by bringing together fragmented insights that have not previously been integrated.

LLM agents increasingly use retrieval tools across languages, yet their safety evaluation remains English-centric. It remains unclear whether language affects tool admission, post-retrieval generation, or both. We independently vary request, retrieved-page, and required response languages in a controlled URL-retrieval setting across ten models and seven languages. We identify Safety Loss through Interlingual Processing (SLIP). Non-English harmful requests increase mean tool admission from 46.9% to 67.4%, with a positive mean change in every model. This pattern also persists in an autonomous retrieval setup across all four models tested in this setting. Requiring answers in the page language increases pooled harmfulness on matched tool calls from 50.3% to 57.4% across four closed-weight models, mainly in Chinese and Hindi. Translating pages alone produces no consistent harm increase in eight models with comparable inference settings. Automated audits show that a non-harmful response may be a genuine safety refusal, a deflection citing language difficulties, or an unusable answer. Harmfulness labels alone cannot distinguish these outcomes. Multilingual safety evaluations should therefore measure tool admission and response harmfulness separately and distinguish refusal from capability failure.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This paper addresses the problem that, during the distillation of large language models, student models may remain at the level of imitating teacher models' answers and struggle to develop stable knowledge-invocation capabilities. It proposes a conceptual architecture for response-structure distillation and teacher–student blind-evaluation post-training, with the aim of developing transferable capabilities. This paper argues that, when two models have similar knowledge bases, differences in response quality may lie more in how knowledge is invoked, organized, and applied than in the amount of knowledge the models possess. Accordingly, this study proposes a distillation-first, training-second sequence in which the response structure is treated as an independent learning target: the student model learns the teacher model's response structures across different contexts, and then invokes its own existing knowledge to fill in those structures. Subsequently, the student model's responses are jointly evaluated through five sources of evaluation—a structure-evaluation model, a scoring model, domain experts, non-experts, and anonymous comparisons between the teacher and student models. The evaluation results and disagreements are fed back to the student model, and through repeated revision and subsequent training, the architecture attempts to gradually consolidate effective ways of invoking knowledge into stable, invocable paths within the student model. This paper further proposes mechanisms such as feeding structure-related feedback back into the revision process, limiting the number of iteration rounds, and generating training signals, so as to form a post-training closed loop of continuous correction. The proposed architecture aims to explore a possible path from imitating the teacher model's way of answering to developing the student model's own answering capabilities; its effectiveness and its ability to transfer to unseen contexts remain to be verified through subsequent experiments.

The digitization of education has concentrated vast volumes of sensitive learner data within centralized platforms that are priority targets for cyber attackers. It is argued that the dominant centralized model of educational artificial intelligence is structurally misaligned with modern privacy and resilience needs, and an alternative grounded in Distributed Artificial Intelligence is proposed. A layered architecture is presented that couples Federated Learning with Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents to deliver privacy-preserving analytics and autonomous cyber resilience without centralizing raw data. Learner records remain on institutional premises; model updates are protected by differential privacy and secure aggregation; and collaborative threat detection and self-healing are performed by distributed BDIx agents. BDIx-FL reached 99.17% accuracy, 98.93% macro-F1 and 99.76% macro AUC in simulation. Controversies are examined, deployment recommendations are offered and open directions are identified for educational ecosystems that are trustworthy by design.

Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.

While data collection for model training is relatively easy, curating high-quality datasets from large collections is inherently challenging. Coreset estimation methods address this problem by identifying the best data subsets to train models on. However, existing approaches often require proxy model training, extensive annotations, or task-specific tailoring. Unsupervised alternatives typically exploit geometric properties in foundation model feature spaces, but are limited to pairwise image-to-image comparisons or comparisons against a fixed subset. We introduce CoreDNA, an unsupervised, task-agnostic coreset estimation approach that pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and per-dataset distributions. By comparing each image's distribution to the dataset-level distribution, CoreDNA can capture both low-level visual structure and high-level semantic information across layers. We find that high-quality samples concentrate in the tails of the last layer's activation statistics, which we validate by relating them to training-based coreset methods. Building on these findings, we develop a computationally efficient selection mechanism to construct task-agnostic, high-quality coresets for selective annotation and model training. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and imitation learning for end-to-end driving and mobile manipulation, CoreDNA matches or outperforms the state of the art, demonstrating unprecedented generalization across perception and action tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact activation-based representations for data selection.

Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms are becoming increasingly prevalent in healthcare. Unlike previous technologies, AI has the capability to perform tasks previously considered uniquely human including synthesizing historical information and data to establish a clinical diagnosis and constructing a treatment plan. AI promises to improve diagnostic accuracy, accelerate drug discovery and development, and enhance access to healthcare. The overall impact that AI will have on the well-being of individuals who provide and receive care, however, is less obvious. This article examines the potential and pitfalls of AI in medicine through the lens of mattering and its importance to human flourishing. Mattering is a psychological construct that encompasses the human needs to be noticed, feel significant, and contribute. It arises from interpersonal interactions and is based on perceptions of our value within our communities and society. Mattering is inherently relational, is a significant contributor to psychological well-being, and may be at risk in the age of AI. The authors describe the foundations of mattering and its relevance to medicine; the potential impacts of AI on mattering in medicine from the clinician, patient, and trainee perspectives; and propose a framework for integrating AI into healthcare such that mattering is preserved for all stakeholders.
