Machine-learned interatomic potentials distilled from foundation models enable fast large-scale molecular dynamics (MD), but they can fail locally in chemical environments that their training data did not sample. System-averaged error metrics and small random audits often miss such sparse or isolated failures. Here we use an exact equivariant foundation model, MACE-MPA-0, to check every atom of million-atom production simulations. Reorganizing two-layer MACE inference into a receiver-chunked three-pass schedule that keeps no per-edge intermediates resident reduces the marginal memory per atom 340-fold, evaluates up to $2.86\times10^{7}$ atoms on a single H200 GPU, and supervises $10^{6}$-atom trajectories in LAMMPS at 1.3% of the run time. Distilled MACE students run four to nine times slower than NEP89 with 0.95-1.28 times the teacher's force error against density functional theory (DFT). In molten SiO$_2$, whole-system checks uncover a persistent tail of under-coordinated atoms hidden by the system-averaged error and an isolated, unphysical O-O contact that a 1% random audit misses 94% of the time. On-the-fly retraining on teacher-labelled 13-Å clusters, with the force loss restricted to their inner 6 Å, removes three quarters of the failure tail and the kilobar-level pressure biases in SiO$_2$ and compressed water; the repair converges to the teacher, not to DFT.

Generative artificial intelligence has changed the conditions under which users encounter and evaluate machine-produced communication. In systems based on large language models, conversational output is no longer merely functional; it can be fluent, context-aware, and socially legible, inviting judgments that extend beyond usefulness, accuracy, or efficiency. Yet the literature still tends to treat anthropomorphism, perceived authenticity, and trust as largely separate constructs, without sufficiently explaining how human-like cues become credible in the eyes of users and how this credibility shapes trust. To address this problem, the present structured literature review synthesizes recent research on anthropomorphism, authenticity-related evaluations, and trust in AI-mediated interaction, with particular attention to conversational AI, generative AI, and LLM-based systems. A structured search in the Web of Science Core Collection identified 655 records; after duplicate removal, screening, and eligibility assessment, 96 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The analysis identifies several interrelated thematic patterns, including anthropomorphic cues and social presence, authenticity-related mechanisms in AI-mediated communication, trust formation and calibration, boundary conditions, and behavioral responses to conversational AI. On this basis, the review develops an integrative conceptual framework and proposes perceived anthropomorphic authenticity as a review-derived construct for examining how users evaluate human-like AI communication in relation to trust. The study contributes to human–AI interaction research by clarifying the role of authenticity-related evaluations between anthropomorphic cues and calibrated trust and by identifying conditions under which human-like communication may be associated with trust, skepticism, overreliance, or trust erosion.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Purpose: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), including tools such as ChatGPT, is increasingly used by university students for explanations, summaries, problem-solving, feedback, and academic support. This paper examines whether such assistance supports learning or may encourage dependence that affects long-term retention and independent thinking. Methods: The study uses secondary research and a descriptive synthesis of published experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. No primary data were collected and no new statistical meta-analysis was conducted. Results: The reviewed studies generally report positive effects on academic performance and engagement. Reported effect sizes include approximately g = 0.712 across 69 experimental studies, Hedges’ g = 0.577 across 37 studies, and an effect size of approximately 0.804 across 57 studies. However, one randomized controlled study reported 45-day retention of 57.5% for a ChatGPT-assisted group compared with 68.5% for a traditional-learning group. Conclusion: GenAI can be a useful learning assistant when students actively use it for explanation, feedback, comparison, and clarification. However, completing tasks efficiently should not be treated as proof of deep or lasting learning. Students should retain opportunities for independent recall, reasoning, analysis, and problem-solving.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The ongoing transformation of the face of modern business and society brought about by Artificial Intelligence (AI), organisations with a paradox: massive possibilities and no less massive threats. Most attempts at digital transformation fail to attain long-term success due to a fragmented approach and human factor resistance, with the potential of AI to provide unmatched efficiencies and innovation. In the current work, the presented approach is called APSS: the practical four-step framework with Awareness, Piloting, Scaling, and Sustainability, which is presented to help companies become successful in the process of implementing the journey of AI adoption. The APSS approach is a strategic, collaborative, value-oriented approach, rather than a technology-focused solution (AI). It starts with the creation of organisational awareness and change preparedness and continues with attempts of AI pilots, to which some business priorities are attached. Successful programs are subsequently extended across the organisation with accurate governance and performance indicators, which results in the application of AI in long-term programs that encourage innovation, agility and sustainability. Using the concept of the academic literature and practice itself, this paper has incorporated change management principles, open innovation, and human-centred design. A case study of one of the Greek technology leaders illustrates the real-life application of the APSS framework, which can be explained by the fact that it is applied to overcome internal resistance, organise cross-functional teams, and produce a measurable business value. This book contributes to the discussion about the responsible AI strategy and offers a practical template that should be followed by any organisation that strives to build the future not only AI-driven but also socially responsible and ethics-grounded.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Healthspan, the period of life free from major chronic disease and disability, is a central geroscience outcome, yet its prediction remains difficult due to its multidimensional and heterogeneous nature. In this review, we synthesize advances in artificial intelligence (AI) for precision healthspan assessment, shifting from chronological age estimates toward physiologically grounded, individualized health trajectory forecasting. We examine supervised, deep, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning approaches, alongside AI-based biomarkers of aging, including epigenetic, proteomic, imaging, and wearable-derived digital biomarkers. We also discuss multimodal AI integrating multi-omic, imaging, and sensor data, explainable AI for clinical translation, and key issues in validation, regulation, ethics, bias, privacy, and equitable access. We critically appraise the level of validation supporting each major technology, distinguish biological-age estimation from true healthspan prediction, and separate predictive performance from demonstrated clinical utility. In this review, we conclude that AI-powered healthspan algorithms hold promise for shifting healthcare from reactive disease management to proactive, personalized aging management, but current evidence remains strongest for prediction and weakest for clinical utility; translation will require rigorous external and prospective validation, standardized outcomes, robust ethical and regulatory frameworks, and equitable implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Genetics, Aging, and Longevity in Model Organisms

documents.abstract: Deepfake detection has advanced rapidly alongside progress in generative adversarial networks, diffusion models, neural rendering, and multimodal synthesis. However, strong performance on curated benchmark datasets does not necessarily translate into reliable performance in real-world environments, where manipulated media are affected by platform compression, reposting, post-processing, multimodal inconsistency, temporal drift, and evolving generation pipelines. This review examines deepfake detection from the perspective of in-the-wild robustness, multimodal reasoning, and cross-domain generalization. It first clarifies the conceptual foundations of in-the-wild and generalizable deepfake detection, then reviews the data ecosystem, including benchmark datasets, real-world media conditions, multimodal data gaps, annotation quality, and benchmark aging. The review further analyzes the major causes of detector failure under realistic deployment conditions, including generator shift, platform-induced degradation, modality mismatch, language and speaker variation, and broader contextual diversity. It then compares major methodological families, including artifact-based methods, deep representation-based approaches, transfer-based learning, domain adaptation, domain generalization, and multimodal detection strategies, with emphasis on their relevance to real-world robustness. Finally, the review discusses evaluation practices, external validation, realistic benchmarking, and future directions such as continually updated benchmarks, missing-modality-robust systems, uncertainty-aware detection, provenance integration, and foundation-model-based approaches. Overall, the review argues that reliable deepfake detection requires a shift from benchmark-centered optimization toward robust, multimodal, and deployment-oriented evaluation and design.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in high-impact domains has heightened concerns regarding the protection of fundamental rights. While the EU AI Act introduces the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) as a key governance mechanism for certain high-risk AI systems, its broader conceptual role remains underexplored. This chapter argues that the FRIA should not be understood merely as a compliance obligation but as an emerging form of human rights auditing for algorithmic systems. Drawing on audit theory, human rights due diligence, and algorithmic accountability scholarship, it develops a conceptual framework that reframes the FRIA as a rights-based assurance mechanism. It further proposes a Rights Safeguards Audit Ladder to assess the maturity of organizational safeguards and illustrates its application through AI-based credit scoring. We contribute to AI governance debates by showing how human rights auditing can bridge the gap between regulatory compliance, organizational accountability, and continuous rights protection in high-risk AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative models for deepfakes have rapidly evolved from GAN-based architectures to diffusion models and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, empirical research on human performance in detecting deepfake face images has not kept pace. It remains unclear if (and how) detection performance varies across generative models and whether model-specific training improves detection more effectively than general-purpose training. In this paper, we propose the \emph{Deepfake Face Artifact Taxonomy} (DFAT), a cross-model taxonomy of human-recognizable visual artifacts in deepfake face images, based on which we build both general-purpose and model-specific training materials. Through an online experiment ($n = 524$), we examined human performance in detecting deepfake face images and evaluated training efficacy across five representative generative models: three GAN-based, one diffusion-based, and one MLLM (GPT-5). Our results show that participants' detection accuracy was strongly model-dependent and that images generated by more recent and advanced models were not necessarily harder to detect. After training, participants achieved significant performance gains across most conditions, and their improvement varied by model. Notably, model-specific training generally yielded greater numerical gains than general-purpose training. In a five-month follow-up test ($n = 342$), we observed no significant decline in detection accuracy and no significant increase in perceived stress. Overall, our findings provide actionable insights for designing effective, sustainable, and targeted training programs to counter the growing threat posed by deepfakes.

Cervical cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women globally, with persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection as the primary etiological factor. Cervical precancerous lesions, including high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions and adenocarcinoma in situ, represent the critical window for intervention prior to invasive cancer development. However, additional factors such as immunosuppression, smoking, and microbiome composition also play crucial roles in the development of cervical precancerous lesions. While HPV vaccination, screening, and treatment have reduced cancer incidence, these must be complemented by personalized approaches that target the molecular mechanisms driving carcinogenesis. Key dysregulated tumor suppressors (e.g., p16) and signaling pathways (PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin) highlight the need for advanced therapeutic strategies. The immune microenvironment also plays a critical role in cancer progression, suggesting potential for immunotherapy. Promising biomarkers like p16, Ki67, and microRNAs require integration with technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics for deeper insights into tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment dynamics. Additionally, while deep learning models hold promise in improving diagnostic accuracy for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN), challenges such as data variability and interpretability need addressing. In conclusion, incorporating genomics, transcriptomics, immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence will enable more personalized and effective interventions, ultimately reducing the global burden of cervical cancer.

Abstract This article develops the concept of a brokered dormitory labor regime (BDLR) to analyze Johor, Malaysia’s electrical and electronics export-processing zones, where debt-financed recruitment, deceptive contracting, and restricted mobility synchronize labor turnover with the accelerating demand for semiconductor manufacturing driven by artificial intelligence. Two intermediaries, the labor agent and the kadar, secure this synchronization by controlling workers’ social reproduction. Tracing this regime’s genealogy to the nineteenth-century kangani and kangchu systems in the Straits Settlements, the article argues that the BDLR reactivates a colonial infrastructure of coerced migrant labor, revealing a recurring pattern of asynchronous synchronization between capital and labor across successive industrial revolutions.

Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and reasoning, but their reliance on static parametric knowledge still leads to knowledge staleness, hallucinations, limited domain adaptability, weak traceability, and high updating costs in knowledge-intensive scenarios. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) helps address these limitations by incorporating external knowledge sources into the generation process, making it an important approach for improving factual grounding, knowledge timeliness, and evidence traceability. However, existing RAG research is increasingly fragmented across architectures, retrieval and generation strategies, evaluation methods, application scenarios, deployment constraints, and security risks. To provide a systematic understanding of this field, this survey reviews RAG research through a structured and transparent review protocol. We organize the review around three major dimensions: the system stack and paradigm evolution of RAG, evaluation methods and application evidence, and practical deployment and security challenges. Specifically, we analyze the core components of RAG systems, synthesize their evolution from Naive RAG to Agentic RAG, examine evaluation metrics and stress-testing protocols, summarize benchmark datasets and domain applications, and discuss deployment constraints and emerging risks such as prompt injection, data poisoning, retrieval hijacking, privacy leakage, and citation laundering. This survey provides a taxonomy-oriented, evaluation-aware, and deployment-conscious reference for understanding the development, limitations, and future directions of RAG systems.

Autonomous AI agents can read sensitive information, execute privileged commands, and move data betweenenterprise systems. Existing authentication and authorization checks remain necessary, but a tool call can be permittedwhile the sequence of calls produces a result outside the authorized business task. This paper addresses a practicalsecurity problem: how can an enterprise detect and stop a harmful sequence of individually permitted actions beforea damaging action executes? It proposes Trajectory-Aware Zero Trust (TA-ZT), a vendor-neutral referencearchitecture that combines DoD Zero Trust pillars, CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model v2, task-scoped authorization,action history, data lineage, and independent policy enforcement. The proposed architecture allows a security gatewayto approve, pause, or deny a sensitive action using both its immediate parameters and its task-level context. The paperexplains the security gap, expected organizational value, control mapping, engineering components, exampleworkflow, test methodology, and phased implementation. It is a conceptual research proposal, not a deployed orexperimentally validated system. Keywords: autonomous AI agents; agentic security; Zero Trust architecture; DoD; CISA; policy decision point; policyenforcement point; task-scoped authorization; trajectory monitoring; data lineage

1. Background In recent years, the escalating global burden of appearance-related distress has transformed social physique anxiety into a multidimensional public health challenge. Although the rapid expansion of digital environments significantly exacerbates appearance vulnerabilities and the volume of academic literature has grown substantially, a comprehensive quantitative mapping of the field's evolutionary trajectory remains lacking. Previous reviews were often limited to a single database, which may result in a biased representation of global trends and fail to capture the core theoretical transition from specific "physique anxiety" (focusing strictly on adiposity and muscularity) to broader "social appearance anxiety" (encompassing global aesthetic evaluations like facial features and skin tone). 2. Objective This project aims to systematically visualize the knowledge structure, spatiotemporal distribution, and developmental trends of social physique anxiety research by integrating literature from the past two decades (January 1, 2006, to August 15, 2026). Specific objectives include: Mapping and evaluating the global collaboration networks among authors, institutions, and countries. Identifying current research hotspots through keyword co-occurrence and structural clustering analyses. Building a dynamic predictive framework via keyword burst detection to forecast emerging frontiers that will shape future targeted behavioral interventions and clinical practice. 3. Methods Summary This study employs bibliometric methods to systematically retrieve and integrate data from two major authoritative databases: Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus. After excluding ineligible data, the records are rigorously cleaned using a Python-based triple-verification deduplication algorithm (BibexPy framework), resulting in a final dataset of 624 unique eligible articles. The harmonized data is then subjected to in-depth network mapping and visualization analysis using CiteSpace and VOSviewer. 4. Expected Results & ImplicationsThis project aims to comprehensively elucidate the structural shifts within this domain over the past two decades, with expected key findings including:Global Contributions and Networks: Highlighting the leadership of countries like Turkey, the United States, and Canada in driving international contributions, and revealing how transnational collaboration networks among highly productive academic institutions advance theoretical progress. Thematic Evolution Trajectories: Delineating the shift in research focus from early instrument development (e.g., psychometric validations) to a contemporary strategic focus on transdiagnostic psychopathology and holistic well-being (quality of life) interventions. Impact of Digital Culture: Highlighting the exacerbating role of modern "digital filter culture" and social media addiction in amplifying appearance-related distress and broader social anxiety among youth. Frontier Interventions: Predicting and emphasizing the emerging potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven personalized psychological interventions, digital phenotyping, and exposure therapies in proactive mental health management. In summary, by delineating established domains such as eating disorder comorbidity and tracking emerging trajectories in digital health, this research provides a vital evidence-based framework for optimizing targeted behavioral interventions. It also emphasizes the core value of protective mechanisms like self-compassion in mitigating negative self-evaluation and promoting exercise adherence.

In this literature narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies for colorectal endoscopy (PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library, January 2015 to June 2026, with supplementary hand-searching), the "pixels-to-prevention" paradigm -image interpretation → detection → characterization → clinical decision → treatment quality → surveillance → prevention -is employed to examine whether the well-evidenced performance characteristics of AI can actually be tied to effective cancer prevention rather than merely listing out the different types of applications of AI that were reported in previous reviews.Colorectal cancer prevention is strongly connected to colonoscopy but is limited by lesion miss rates, endoscopist variability, and interpretation of the results into management.Computer-aided detection enhances the adenoma detection rates and reduces the lesion miss rate, but the higher adenoma detection rates is just a surrogate and does not directly contribute to cancer prevention: AI-assisted colonoscopy prefers the detection of diminutive and non-neoplastic lesions rather than advanced neoplasms.This review traces the evolution from computer-aided detection to computer-aided characterization and optical diagnosis, highlighting their recent applications for quality control of resection, prediction of recurrence development, and individualized surveillance based on risk stratification where we distinguish advances in metrics of performance from clinical utility (interval colorectal cancer, unneeded resections, surveillance burden).The review considers the questions related to the problem of false positives, algorithm bias, dataset variability, lack of external validation, automation bias, interpretability, workflow, and regulation.Asking ourselves how intelligent endoscopy could help us going beyond the discovery of lesions through the use of artificial intelligence, we propose an agenda for research that focuses on validation and patient outcome.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants' accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

Artificial intelligence has evolved from rule-based symbolic systems into learning architectures capable of perception, prediction, content generation, reasoning, planning, tool use, and increasingly autonomous action. This qualitative literature review examines this transition as more than a technological chronology. It interprets AI evolution through five interrelated dimensions: technological evolution, capability expansion, changing human roles, human–AI integration, and governance. Drawing on contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2020 and 2026, the review identifies seven thematic developments. AI has progressed from encoded rules toward learned representations and goal-directed action; generative AI has expanded AI into a general-purpose content collaborator; agentic AI adds planning, memory, tool use, and iterative task execution; human roles increasingly shift from operator toward collaborator, delegator, and governor; human–AI complementarity remains conditional rather than automatic; effective deployment requires calibrated rather than maximal trust; and governance requirements increase as AI systems acquire greater operational agency. The article proposes the Evolution–Capability–Role–Integration–Governance (ECRIG) framework to explain these relationships. The framework suggests that sustainable benefits from advanced AI emerge when technological capability, human role allocation, interaction architecture, and governance mechanisms develop jointly. The review concludes that the central challenge of the agentic-AI era is not choosing between humans and machines, but designing accountable systems in which increasingly capable artificial agents remain aligned with meaningful human goals, authority, and oversight.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Professional identity formation (PIF) is increasingly understood as a socially situated workplace learning process through which medical students develop identities and practices of physicians. Through participation in clinical work within the clinical learning environment (CLE), students learn what it means to become members of the profession. Within this context, a sense of belonging may be an important mechanism linking the CLE to PIF. However, quantitative evidence examining these relationships remains limited. This study examined whether sense of belonging mediates the relationship between the CLE and PIF. METHODS: This cross-sectional study used data from 459 undergraduate clinical students in Indonesia collected between November 1 and December 15, 2024. Students completed three validated instruments: the Professional Identity Formation (PIF) questionnaire, the Undergraduate Clinical Education Environment Measure (UCEEM), and the Belongingness Scale-Clinical Placement Experience (BES-CPE). Structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to assess whether sense of belonging functioned as a mediator between the CLE and PIF. RESULTS: < 0.001). The SEM mediation model demonstrated good fit (SRMR = 0.038, CFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.94), indicating that belonging partially mediated the relationship between the CLE and PIF. DISCUSSION: The findings reveal that PIF are positively linked to both CLE and a sense of belonging. In addition, sense of belonging functions as a significant statistical mediator in the pathway linking the CLE to PIF. These findings suggest that workplace learning experiences contribute to PIF not only directly but also through fostering students' sense of belonging. Creating supportive clinical environments that promote participation, inclusion, and membership may therefore strengthen medical students' PIF.

Within this context, a sense of belonging may be an important mechanism linking the CLE to PIF. However, quantitative evidence examining these relationships remains limited. This study examined whether sense of belonging mediates the relationship between the CLE and PIF. This cross-sectional study used data from 459 undergraduate clinical students in Indonesia collected between November 1 and December 15, 2024. Students completed three validated instruments: the Professional Identity Formation (PIF) questionnaire, the Undergraduate Clinical Education Environment Measure (UCEEM), and the Belongingness Scale-Clinical Placement Experience (BES-CPE). Structural equation modelling (SEM) was employed to assess whether sense of belonging functioned as a mediator between the CLE and PIF. PIF showed a moderate positive correlation with both the CLE (r = 0.416; p < 0.001) and sense of belonging (r = 0.370; p < 0.001), while the CLE was strongly correlated to sense belonging (r = 0.578; p < 0.001). The SEM mediation model demonstrated good fit (SRMR = 0.038, CFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.94), indicating that belonging partially mediated the relationship between the CLE and PIF. The findings reveal that PIF are positively linked to both CLE and a sense of belonging. In addition, sense of belonging functions as a significant statistical mediator in the pathway linking the CLE to PIF. These findings suggest that workplace learning experiences contribute to PIF not only directly but also through fostering students’ sense of belonging. Creating supportive clinical environments that promote participation, inclusion, and membership may therefore strengthen medical students’ PIF.

Population ageing in the workforce is one of the key challenges for contemporary labour markets. This article aims to present and critically evaluate a conceptual model for assessing the risk of reduced or discontinued employment among individuals aged ≥55 years. The study is a review based on an integrative synthesis of literature on work ability, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, job crafting, work design, and research on retention and return to work. The proposed model is based on an employee functional profile and a task-matching matrix. It assumes task-level analysis of work, with tasks assessed in terms of physical, cognitive, emotional, and social demands, as well as organizational and personal value. Based on this, 4 types of organizational decisions are identified: task maintenance, workload reduction, task redistribution, and task enrichment. The model enables the identification of risk configurations, such as accumulation of demands, erosion of work value, impaired recovery, environmental mismatch, and underuse of competences. However, it is not a validated predictive tool. The proposed framework supports the design of work that promotes longer, healthier, and more sustainable working lives among workers aged ≥55 years. Further empirical validation and sector-specific adaptation are required. Med Pr Work Health Saf. 2026;77(5).

The rapid expansion of digital technologies has fundamentally altered the manner in which individuals communicate, access information, participate in public life, conduct economic activities, and exercise personal autonomy. The transition from an analogue to a digitally mediated society has consequently transformed the environment in which fundamental rights operate. In India, constitutional guarantees contained in Part III of the Constitution were originally formulated in an era preceding the internet, social media, artificial intelligence, biometric identification, algorithmic decision-making and large-scale data processing. Nevertheless, the constitutional framework has demonstrated considerable capacity to respond to technological change through judicial interpretation, particularly by expanding the meaning of liberty, privacy and dignity under Article 21 of Constitution of India. The Apex Court of India has played an important role in this constitutional transformation. Land mark judgments such as Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India and K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) v. Union of India have contributed to the development of a fundamental rights-based understanding of digital governance and technological freedom. At the same time, the emergence of artificial intelligence, facial recognition, pervasive surveillance, data profiling, deepfakes, online harassment, misinformation and platform-based censorship presents challenges that cannot always be addressed through traditional interpretations of constitutional rights. This paper examines how fundamental rights and human rights must be understood in the digital era, with particular emphasis on Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India. As these three articles are golden triangle, stated under Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India case. It argues that digital constitutionalism requires the protection of not merely physical freedom but also informational autonomy, decisional freedom, digital expression, anonymity, personal identity and human dignity. The paper further examines the relationship between privacy and national security, freedom of speech and online regulation, and technological innovation and constitutional accountability. It concludes that technological advancement must remain compatible with constitutional morality, proportionality, transparency, accountability and the dignity of the individual.

Abstract Background Preclinical dental training emphasizes indirect vision using mirrors for precision and ergonomics to prevent musculoskeletal disorders. Students often face challenges with suboptimal posture and extended procedure times. Digital gamified tools like mobile app and ImageJ software enable objective and repeatable assessments, although targeted studies on indirect vision improvement remain limited. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of digital training in improving precision of performance and ergonomic posture during indirect vision tasks. Aim To assess the impact of gamified smartphone training on indirect vision skills in preclinical BDS students. Methods The aim of this study was to assess the impact of gamified smartphone training on indirect vision skills in preclinical BDS students. Parallel RCT at Manipal College of Dental Sciences, Mangalore ( n = 68 s-year BDS; control n = 34, intervention n = 34). Intervention group: Total 40 min, with each session 20-min with break Pac-Man 256 indirect mirror training on personal device. Both: Standardized phantom head cavity outline coloring. Outcomes: ImageJ % error (v1.54p), time (min), and modified CADEP score.Shapiro-Wilk test for normality and Mann-Whitney U test for group comparisons. Results 87.5% (14/16) of the variables were non-normal ( p < 0.05) in both groups. The training group showed reduced time, lower error, and superior CADEP scores compared to the controls ( p < 0.05). Conclusion Brief gamified digital training significantly improves indirect vision, efficiency, and ergonomics of dental students. Overall, gamified cellular device-based indirect vision training improved the accuracy of cavity preparation. We recommend low-cost integration into undergraduate curricula. Trial registration The study was Retrospectively registered with the Clinical Trials Registry - India (CTRI), CTRI Reg. Date 27/07/2026 with registration number CTRI/2026/07/114,792.

This study examined the conditions that enable or constrain undergraduate students’ access to, and meaningful use of, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at a rural South African university. Using an interpretivist qualitative case study design, researchers conducted semi-structured, face-to-face interviews with 12 undergraduate students with prior experience using GenAI for academic purposes. Data were analysed thematically following Braun and Clarke’s ix-phase approach. Four interconnected conditions shaped students’ experiences: device and connectivity reliability, the affordability of sustained data access, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, and institutional infrastructure and training. Students consistently perceived GenAI as useful, but their capacity to realise that usefulness depended on resources and competencies that were unevenly distributed. The study uses this gap to extend TAM’s construct of perceived usefulness with a distinct construct of realised usefulness, and this study argues that generative AI introduces a literacy demand, critical evaluation of machine-generated, plausible-sounding but sometimes inaccurate output. The study contributes to digital-inequality scholarship by extending the access–skills–benefits distinction into the generative AI context and by identifying the gap between perceived and realised usefulness as a mechanism through which existing inequalities may be reproduced. The study recommends that institutional responses combine connectivity, affordable access, structured AI literacy instruction, and explicit academic guidance, rather than treating any one of these as sufficient on its own.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Decision making in business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce connects company and consumer activities before, during and after purchase, whereas many existing generative artificial intelligence (GAI) applications focus on specific tasks or functions. This article develops a conceptual framework linking employee responsibilities, consumer choices, GAI support, information sources, permissions and two-sided evaluation through the five-stage Consumer Buying Behaviour (CBB) process. It connects need clarification, information gathering, feasible-offer comparison, transaction review and post-purchase assessment through decision gates and bounded support functions. Five employees and three consumers participated in a fixed-order ChatGPT 5.6 demonstration to examine the administration and perceived value of the proposed decision-support approach. Following a brief GAI introduction, participants observed ordinary prompt-response support and then a structured CBB-guided sequence within the same general e-commerce decision context. Questionnaire ratings were generally more favourable following CBB guidance, particularly for perceived comparison support and mental effort. The study-specific items are descriptive indicators, and fixed ordering confounds condition with practice, familiarity, novelty, fatigue, expectancy and task-set effects. The contribution is strictly conceptual and methodological; the eight-participant exercise supplies procedural illustration and design input, without establishing effectiveness, deployment readiness or validated system behaviour. Future evaluation requires an implemented system, versioned tasks and outputs, independently scored task-level records, and randomised or counterbalanced comparison.

Generative AI tools that condense texts into summaries have become a routine part of student reading routines, and educators increasingly worry that convenient summaries displace the effortful processing on which deep comprehension depends. This study drew on cognitive offloading theory and the levels-of-processing framework to test a moderated mediation model in which elaborative processing statistically links generative AI summarization tool use to deep reading comprehension, and reading motivation moderates the negative association between tool use and processing. Undergraduate students ( N = 608; 53.6% female; mean age 19.9 years) from three universities in Changchun, China, completed a six-item scale of generative AI summarization tool use, an eight-item elaborative processing scale adapted from the deep-processing subscale of the R-SPQ-2F, a seven-item reading motivation measure adapted from the Motivation for Reading Questionnaire, and a researcher-developed deep reading comprehension test. Scale reliabilities were satisfactory (Cronbach alpha = 0.88, 0.87, and 0.86). Tool use correlated negatively with elaborative processing ( r = −0.41) and comprehension ( r = −0.24); elaborative processing correlated positively with comprehension ( r = 0.59). PROCESS analyses (Model 7) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples showed that tool use negatively predicted elaborative processing ( b = −0.310, p < 0.001) and that this association weakened as reading motivation rose (interaction b = 0.433, p < 0.001). Elaborative processing, in turn, predicted comprehension ( b = 10.097, p < 0.001), whereas the residual direct path of tool use did not reach significance. The indirect effect of tool use on comprehension through elaborative processing was significant and negative at low (−6.142, 95% BC CI [−7.353, −5.091]) and average (−3.130, [−3.851, −2.497]) reading motivation but nonsignificant at high reading motivation (−0.117, [−0.876, 0.629]); the index of moderated mediation was 4.374 [3.428, 5.402]. These results are consistent with an account in which elaborative processing statistically links summary reliance to lower deep reading, with reading motivation associated with a weaker negative indirect association; given the cross-sectional design, the modeled paths represent associations rather than established causal effects. They suggest that motivation-oriented reading instruction should accompany, rather than follow, the integration of AI tools into academic reading.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) use and online information checking may be socially patterned in different ways. This cross-sectional study analysed the 2025 Turkish Statistical Institute ICT survey of 22,502 internet users aged 16–74 using weighted modified Poisson regression with household-clustered standard errors. Overall, 19.2% reported generative AI use, and 48.3% of respondents who noticed doubtful content did not check it. Conditional non-checking (the verification gap) increased with age and decreased with education and reported digital activity, whereas AI use followed the opposite pattern. Compared with ages 16–24, the adjusted prevalence ratio at ages 65–74 was 1.48 (95% confidence interval 1.30–1.68) for non-checking and 0.10 (0.07–0.16) for AI use. Health information seekers and AI users reported less non-checking among those who noticed doubtful content, but neither group had a lower prevalence of noticing without checking among all internet users. Among non-checkers, 87.3% reported already judging the information or source unreliable and 15.2% reported insufficient skills or knowledge; responses could overlap. These findings distinguish participation in AI use, reported noticing of doubtful content, and subsequent checking. Verification support should address reported difficulty separately from decisions not to investigate content already considered unreliable.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This white paper examines how generative AI use in workplace workflows can lead to destructive system actions, defective professional work, and unauthorized disclosure of restricted information. Its central assessment is that approving an AI tool or assigning a human reviewer does not establish control of the complete workflow. Drawing on Replit, Mata v. Avianca, and Deloitte, with Samsung included as a qualified reported incident, the paper traces how task definition, permissions, information handling, and human–AI interaction turn actions and outputs into business consequences. It distinguishes documented incidents from experimental research, technical evidence, and proposed safeguards. The analysis provides recommendations for validating objectives, restricting access and transmission, testing human review, and evaluating final outcomes. It identifies conditions supporting workflow expansion, restriction, or suspension. Written for security, governance, risk, operations, and professional-services leaders, the paper includes Chicago-style endnotes and a bibliography.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) promises to transform supply chain disruption management, yet its cognitive benefits and associated governance tensions remain insufficiently understood. This study conceptualises and empirically examines a cognitive paradox whereby GenAI accelerates managerial sensemaking, expands response options, and facilitates adaptive reframing while increasing verification demands, accountability uncertainty, and coordination difficulties. Using a scenario-based mixed-methods design, the research integrates an experiment with 200 senior supply chain managers randomly assigned to GenAI-supported and unsupported decision environments and 25 executive interviews. The study examines cognitive agility, operationalised through rapid reframing, information integration, and evaluative flexibility, as the managerial mechanism linking GenAI support to disruption-response effectiveness. Experimental findings associate GenAI support with greater cognitive agility and improved decision accuracy, adaptability, and timeliness. Exploratory Bayesian network analysis identifies complementary probabilistic dependencies without establishing causality. Qualitative evidence demonstrates that these benefits depend on data integration, verification practices, calibrated trust, managerial competence, and explicit decision rights. The study contributes to supply chain scholarship by establishing cognitive agility as a microfoundation of GenAI-enabled disruption response and identifying governance maturity as a boundary condition distinguishing cognitive augmentation from accelerated error, accountability ambiguity, and coordination failure.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) provides a promising way to acquire language-guided visual representations for Sign Language Translation (SLT). However, the unique temporal characteristics of sign language videos hinder the effective utilization of text supervisory signals. In this paper, we re-examine the impact of different text data on guiding visual feature extraction in VLP, demonstrating that text more temporally aligned with the videos yields more informative supervision. Based on this finding, we propose a Context-aware Dynamic Semantic Enhancement (CDSE) method to enhance text supervision. CDSE enables text data to simulate the temporal characteristics of the videos by integrating data-driven statistical properties with an adaptive expansion mechanism. Moreover, to reduce text annotation costs, we inject sign language priors into Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo-gloss sequences from spoken language sentences. We further design a multi-positive contrastive learning method to mitigate the adverse effects of individual low-quality pseudo-glosses. Extensive experiments on two widely used datasets, PHOENIX14T (8257 videos) and CSL-Daily (20,654 videos), demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the baseline. On the test sets of both datasets, our method improves BLEU-4 by 2.53 and 2.82 points, and ROUGE by 2.48 and 2.08 points, respectively.

Artificial intelligence (AI)-based mineral prospectivity mapping (MPM) has rapidly advanced through the integration of deep learning, multisource geoscience data, and increasingly complex representation-learning approaches. However, the reliability of AI-derived prospectivity predictions remains a critical challenge because high predictive performance does not necessarily indicate geological validity, spatial transferability, or exploration usefulness. The key challenge is therefore not model complexity, but aligning geological knowledge, data representation, validation, and uncertainty assessment to ensure reliable interpretation. This review provides a structured critical synthesis of geological reliability in deep learning-based MPM, focusing on the methodological factors that influence whether AI outputs can support defensible exploration decisions. Rather than comparing algorithms solely by predictive accuracy, we examine the interconnected roles of geological representation, prediction support, label construction, negative-sample strategies, validation design, uncertainty quantification, explainability, transferability, and independent geological verification. Assessment of representative AI-based MPM studies reveals inconsistent reporting of these reliability dimensions, limiting reproducibility and meaningful comparison across studies. The review identifies recurring reliability bottlenecks, including spatial leakage caused by inappropriate validation strategies, uncertainty introduced during evidence-layer construction, ambiguity associated with unlabelled geological regions, and limitations in interpreting model explanations as geological causality. To organize these challenges, we propose a hierarchical evidence framework consisting of eight levels: methodological feasibility, internally validated predictive performance, spatial or temporal transferability, geological coherence, calibrated uncertainty, independent geological evidence, prospective field or drilling evidence, and demonstrated decision value. This framework clarifies the strength of claims that can be supported by different levels of evidence and provides a basis for transparent reporting and reliability assessment. Future progress in AI-based MPM will require integration of predictive capability with geological knowledge, robust validation, uncertainty-aware modelling, interpretable predictions, and independent geological verification. The proposed framework aims to support the development of more reproducible, transferable, and decision-relevant AI-assisted mineral exploration workflows.

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly advanced instruction-driven perception through the "Embedding-as-Mask" paradigm. However, extending this capability to Remote Sensing (RS) reasoning segmentation remains exceptionally challenging under cluttered geographical contexts and extreme scale variations, often leading to Spatial Fidelity Degradation and Target Misidentification. We identify a critical yet underexplored bottleneck: the sequential alienation of the segmentation token [SEG] from its initial visual grounding within the autoregressive generation paradigm. Produced only at the end of long reasoning chains, [SEG] relies on visual evidence that has been progressively diluted by linguistic abstraction and autoregressive noise. This information decay is particularly catastrophic for RS targets with minuscule pixel footprints, where even marginal fidelity loss leads to localization failure. To address these bottlenecks, we propose GeoReason, a novel framework designed to fortify logical deduction and preserve spatial integrity. First, we introduce an Anticipatory Prior mechanism that injects the [SEG] token directly into the initial user query, shifting it from a terminal output to a primary condition. This paradigm shift transforms the token into a persistent spatial anchor, preventing information decay during long-form linguistic inference. Second, we enhance visual reasoning via a Location-aware Chain-of-Thought (CoT) that enforces coarse-to-fine localization using bounding boxes, coupled with a Latent Patch-to-Token Alignment (PTA) Loss that explicitly aligns the latent segmentation token with physical RS textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GeoReason consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the Earthreason and RRSIS-D benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanc0126/GeoReason.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This closing discussion seeks to draw out the larger questions about higher education's role in this current moment of AI technology debates, based on the takeaways and ideas for next steps by presenters at this summit. This year's summit submissions centered on practical, classroom-level questions such as: how do we structure assignments so AI supports rather than replaces thinking, how do we teach students to catch AI's confident errors, and how do we build institutional policy on articulated values rather than reactive rules? The presentations on these questions arrive at a moment of a much larger and more unsettled conversation. This year has seen prominent AI researchers — including some from the companies building these systems — publicly disagree about whether increasingly autonomous AI agents pose risks at the scale of catastrophic societal disruption. We cannot resolve that debate here, and none of this summit's sessions were designed to, but this is the backdrop against which conversations about AI in knowledge creation now takes place. This closing discussion asks about the role of higher education when the tools adopted are described, even by some building them, as not fully understood and possibly dangerous — and what needs to be taught about AI now in higher education. Presenters: Dialogue Facilitator: Yvonne Houy Panelists: Nakisa Ghanbarian, Diana Moss, Elisabeth Linn, Elena Azadbakht, Sushma Alphonsa, Brock Casselman, Zachary Porter, Alethea Inns, Jean Hyo Jin Jeon, Sierra Adare-Tasiwoopa api, Michael Chamberlain, Jesse Fitts, Delight Ejiaka Objectives: Synthesize cross-session themes into actionable guidance Examine how classroom practice connects to unresolved, higher-stakes AI questions Surface areas of consensus and disagreement among panelists regarding higher education's role Activities: Facilitated dialogue among summit contributors, drawing on their session findings, followed by open discussion. Expected Outcomes: Participants will leave with ideas for weighing pedagogical decisions against broader uncertainties in AI development, along with possible next steps.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the global banking landscape, acting as a catalyst for innovation and sustainability. This research paper examines the impact of AI on banking sustainability, with a particular focus on its role in driving innovation and enhancing customer engagement. The study analyzes how AI technologies—such as chatbots, predictive analytics, fraud detection systems, and personalized financial services—contribute to operational efficiency, environmental responsibility, and social inclusivity in banking institutions. A mixed-method research design was employed, incorporating case studies of three global banks, a customer survey involving 500 respondents, and 10 expert interviews with banking and AI professionals. The findings indicate that AI-enabled innovations reduce paper usage, improve risk management, optimize resource allocation, and streamline customer service, thereby supporting environmental and operational sustainability. The study also demonstrates that AI enhances customer experience through personalization, accessibility, and trust in digital banking platforms. However, challenges related to data privacy, ethical concerns, and digital exclusion remain significant. The paper concludes by emphasizing the need to align AI adoption with key Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production), and SDG 13 (Climate Action), to ensure that technological advancement in banking supports long-term sustainable development.

Introduction: Polysomnography technologists perform overnight sleep studies requiring continuous patient monitoring, technical management of diagnostic equipment, and sustained attention.Although night-shift work has been associated with adverse health outcomes among healthcare workers, the occupational health burden among polysomnography technologists remains poorly characterized in India.This study evaluated sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, burnout-related symptoms, musculoskeletal symptoms, and selected cardiometabolic indicators and examined their associations with years of night-shift work experience.Methods: This cross-sectional observational study used an online structured questionnaire distributed through professional groups to polysomnography technologists working in private hospitals and sleep centers in South India.Participants were graduates with at least six months of night-shift experience.Of 196 responses, 16 were excluded for less than six months of night-shift experience and 30 for incomplete questionnaires, leaving 150 participants for analysis.The questionnaire included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), and musculoskeletal assessment.Height and weight were measured by participants.Blood pressure was manually assessed, while fasting blood glucose and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) were obtained from recent laboratory reports.Poor sleep quality was defined as PSQI >5 and excessive daytime sleepiness as ESS >10.The CBI was analyzed continuously and categorized operationally as 0-49, 50-74, and 75-100.Years of night-shift work experience were analyzed as a continuous exposure and categorized as ≤5 versus >5 years.Multivariable logistic regression was adjusted for age, sex, and BMI.Results: Mean age was 29.97 ± 4.43 years, and BMI was 24.16 ± 3.19 kg/m².Mean PSQI, ESS, and CBI scores were 7.09 ± 2.95, 9.20 ± 3.39, and 45.99 ± 20.95, respectively.Poor sleep quality occurred in 97 (64.7%), excessive daytime sleepiness in 56 (37.3%), and musculoskeletal symptoms in 126 (84.0%).CBI scores were categorized as 0-49 in 86 (57.3%), 50-74 in 48 (32.0%), and 75-100 in 16 (10.7%).Hypertension-range blood pressure was identified in 21 (14.0%) and prediabetes in 11 (7.3%).Each additional year of night-shift work experience was associated with higher odds of poor sleep quality (adjusted odds ratio (aOR): 1.433, 95% CI: 1.118-1.835),excessive daytime sleepiness (aOR: 1.205, 95% CI: 1.001-1.450),CBI ≥50 (aOR: 1.810, 95% CI: 1.350-2.428),musculoskeletal symptoms (aOR: 1.372, 95% CI: 1.003-1.878),lower-back symptoms (aOR: 1.296, 95% CI: 1.051-1.598),neck symptoms (aOR: 1.272, 95% CI: 1.043-1.552),and hypertension-range blood pressure (aOR: 1.387, 95% CI: 1.052-1.829).No significant associations were observed with shoulder symptoms or prediabetes.Conclusion: Polysomnography technologists reported frequent poor sleep quality, excessive daytime sleepiness, burnout-related symptoms, and musculoskeletal symptoms.More years of night-shift work experience were associated with several adverse health outcomes after adjustment for age, sex, and BMI.These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the cross-sectional design and potential residual confounding.Prospective multicenter studies are warranted.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Assessment in higher education has long centered on core principles such as validity, authenticity, and alignment with learning outcomes, alongside ongoing debates about how best to support academic integrity and meaningful feedback. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now placing renewed pressure on these established principles, prompting institutions to reconsider how assessment is designed, delivered, and evaluated. While a growing body of research has examined GenAI’s role in teaching and learning broadly, less synthesis exists on how it is reshaping assessment specifically, and how these shifts relate to long-standing assessment theory and practice. This systematic review provides an up-to-date examination of empirical research published between 2024 and 2026 on how GenAI is influencing assessment practices and supporting educators in assessing student learning. Using PRISMA, 72 studies were identified and analyzed. The findings show that research was conducted across 24 countries and 20 academic disciplines. Two overarching research purposes emerged: (1) investigating the use of GenAI in assessment and (2) examining perceptions of GenAI in assessment. Qualitative approaches were the most common research methodology. Three major assessment design approaches emerged in response to GenAI: (1) process orientation, (2) authenticity, and (3) oral and dialogical approaches. Five ways educators used GenAI across the assessment process were identified: (1) creating assessments, (2) practice for assessments, (3) grading, (4) transparency of learning, and (5) feedback. Together, these findings situate GenAI’s influence with the broader trajectory of assessment scholarship and provides researchers, educators, institutional leaders, and policymakers a clearer picture of how assessment practices are being negotiated in response to GenAI

Human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) is biologically and clinically distinct from HPV-independent disease. Classically, HPV-associated OPSCC is nonkeratinizing in morphology, less desmoplastic in stroma, and more lymphoid-rich in background; however, it is increasingly recognized as histologically heterogeneous. Keratinizing, maturing, basaloid, papillary, lymphoepithelial, glandular, and other components can be encountered in an HPV-associated tumor, and recent evidence suggests that such micromorphological diversity may be prognostically significant after HPV association has been demonstrated through established assays. In contrast, research from Arab populations has focused largely on HPV prevalence, p16 expression, genotype, and clinical outcome rather than on detailed histology or tumor organization. This critical review synthesizes evidence from Arab countries (focused on Syria) into the contemporary international literature and suggests a regional framework for understanding HPV-associated OPSCC pathology. Studies from Jordan, Lebanon, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates have demonstrated HPV-related or p16-positive OPSCC, with widely varying estimates due to differing anatomical selection and testing strategies. Syrian studies identify high-risk HPV in head-and-neck squamous carcinomas but have not yet estimated the HPV-attributable fraction or histology of anatomically verified Syrian OPSCC. We speculate that future regional research should shift from dichotomous HPV categorization to quantitative characterization of squamous maturation, tumor architecture, stromal response, tumor-associated lymphocytes, front of invasion morphology, and spatial tumor heterogeneity. Digital pathology and interpretable artificial intelligence offer exciting opportunities to engage with these questions. A principal unresolved regional question is the extent and biological significance of HPV involvement in oropharyngeal SCCs, while an important research challenge is to understand how HPV-associated carcinogenesis is expressed through regional variations in tissue architecture.
keywords: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

documents.abstract: The human gut microbiota has emerged as a critical regulator of drug metabolism, therapeutic efficacy, and adverse drug reactions, highlighting its pivotal role in personalized pharmacotherapy. Comprising trillions of microorganisms with diverse metabolic capabilities, the gut microbiome functions as an additional metabolic organ capable of biotransforming numerous therapeutic agents through enzymatic processes such as reduction, hydrolysis, deconjugation, and demethylation. These microbial activities can alter drug absorption, bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and toxicity, thereby contributing to significant interindividual variability in treatment outcomes. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the bidirectional interactions between gut microbiota and drugs, emphasizing their implications for precision medicine and individualized therapeutic strategies. A systematic literature survey was conducted using peer-reviewed publications retrieved from major scientific databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, focusing on studies investigating microbiota-mediated drug metabolism, pharmacomicrobiomics, and microbiome-based therapeutic interventions. The review discusses the composition and physiological functions of the gut microbiota, the molecular mechanisms underlying microbial drug metabolism, and clinically significant interactions involving cardiovascular drugs, antidiabetic agents, anticancer therapies, antibiotics, central nervous system drugs, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Furthermore, recent advances in pharmacomicrobiomics, microbiome-derived biomarkers, artificial intelligence, multi-omics technologies, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation are critically evaluated as emerging approaches for optimizing personalized pharmacotherapy. Despite substantial progress, several challenges, including inter-individual microbial variability, lack of standardized analytical methodologies, limited clinical validation, and regulatory constraints, continue to impede the clinical implementation of microbiome-guided therapy. Future research integrating microbiome profiling with pharmacogenomics, metabolomics, and artificial intelligence is expected to improve the prediction of drug response, minimize adverse drug reactions, and facilitate the development of precision medicine. Overall, gut microbiota–drug interactions represent a promising frontier in pharmaceutical sciences, offering new opportunities to enhance therapeutic efficacy and advance individualized patient care.

Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) architecture is a foundational control pattern for enterprise Artificial Intelligence where AI systems assist with analysis, recommendations, content generation, or task execution while designated people retain authority at critical decision points. As Generative AI and Agentic AI become more autonomous, enterprises require a systematic architecture for determining when human review is mandatory, how work is routed, what evidence reviewers receive, how approvals are recorded, and how overrides and escalations are governed. This paper proposes a Human-in-the-Loop Enterprise AI Architecture integrating AI models, RAG, enterprise data, policy engines, workflow orchestration, identity, approval services, audit trails, security, Responsible AI, and operational monitoring. It defines risk-based review patterns, confidence thresholds, exception routing, separation of duties, and measurable governance controls. The architecture enables organizations to balance automation and human judgment while improving safety, accountability, explainability, compliance, and enterprise trust.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Urban infrastructure shapes environmental quality not only through its form and function but also through the materials from which it is built. Asphalt is a prominent example: heat, solar radiation, and aging can amplify emissions from this climate‐responsive, chemically active material. However, urban air‐quality frameworks continue to treat these emissions as diffuse ambient burdens, overlooking their role as localized, episodic exposure events with potential implications for community health, occupational safety, and functional performance. This review synthesizes evidence across materials science, atmospheric chemistry, exposure science, toxicology, and human factors to propose a unified, human‐centered monitoring framework that links asphalt emission dynamics to exposure conditions, biological relevance, and functional human‐response endpoints. We identify three gaps that motivate the framework: (1) weak integration between emission chemistry, chemical changes and reactions, and real‐world exposure conditions, (2) insufficient monitoring resolution to capture short‐duration, source‐proximate, high‐intensity events, and (3) limited coupling of exposure data with repeated human response measurements and functional endpoints such as symptoms, perception, cognition, and behavior. By organizing these gaps within a single monitoring logic, the framework can guide future efforts to identify who is exposed, under what environmental conditions, and with what potential health or functional relevance. This structure provides a pathway toward more health‐protective infrastructure design, construction practices, and governance. This need is particularly relevant in rapidly urbanizing, arid, and hot‐climate regions, where persistent thermal forcing may amplify both material emissions and human exposure. Although the evidence synthesized in this review focuses primarily on asphalt, the source–exposure–response framework may be transferable to other climate‐sensitive infrastructure materials as part of broader efforts to advance healthier, more adaptive, and more sustainable urban environments.

documents.abstract: Although loss of control (not under command, NUC) is one of the leading triggers of maritime accidents, the quantitative role of human and organizational factors in the process by which it evolves into a risk of grounding and collision has been largely neglected. Traditional approaches primarily treat this situation as a technical reliability issue; however, whether a loss of control leads to a disaster is often determined not by the failure itself, but by human and organizational performance in the first few minutes following the failure. To address this gap, this study proposes an original hybrid methodological framework that combines LLM-supported HFACS-PV coding, Monte Carlo simulation, and decision tree analysis within a sequential and integrated data flow. Within this framework the predictive and quantitative burden rests on the Monte Carlo simulation, while the decision tree contributes an interpretable, descriptive account of factor combinations; it is not presented as a validated predictive classifier. NUC cases compiled from publicly available accident investigation reports were coded into five HFACS-PV layers using a large language model-supported protocol; the resulting layer load was converted into a human factor multiplier that scales the vessel’s time to regain power and fed into the probabilistic simulation as input. The simulation predicts the likelihood of catastrophic outcomes following a loss of control and highlights how the critical time window for intervention narrows significantly—particularly in extreme scenarios—emphasizing the decisive role of initial response capacity. A controlled sensitivity analysis shows that, when physical variables are held constant, the human factor significantly alters the probability of a catastrophic event; however, this effect acts as a conditional modulator dependent on the available time window. Decision tree analysis reveals that the simultaneous occurrence of technology–interface failures and skill-based errors is the pattern most strongly associated with catastrophic outcomes. This decision-tree finding is descriptive and exploratory in nature; under leave-one-out cross-validation the model does not outperform the majority-class baseline and is therefore not used as a predictive classifier. Furthermore, deficiencies in organizational processes and safety management systems emerged as the dominant latent condition in the vast majority of cases, and independent cases outside the dataset also confirmed this trend. The proposed framework offers a practical and comparative decision-support tool that integrates text-based human factor analysis with probabilistic risk modeling.

Fruit quality assessment is important for maintaining postharvest quality, reducing losses and improving the efficiency of sorting and grading operations. Conventional destructive methods provide reliable measurements of physicochemical, chemical, mechanical and microbiological attributes, but generally require sample preparation, laboratory analysis and destruction of the fruit. Non-destructive techniques such as visual inspection, machine vision, near-infrared spectroscopy, multispectral imaging, thermal imaging and electronic nose systems have been increasingly used for fruit quality evaluation, although their ability to provide detailed spatial and spectral information simultaneously is limited. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) combines imaging and spectroscopy to acquire spatially resolved spectral information from intact fruits, allowing both internal quality attributes and external defects to be assessed. This review discusses the development and working principles of HSI, scanning and illumination modes, and the major steps involved in spectral data processing, including preprocessing, feature extraction, wavelength selection and dimensionality reduction. Applications of HSI for internal quality attributes such as soluble solids content, pH, firmness and total soluble solids, as well as external defects and fungal diseases, are reviewed with emphasis on spectral range, data analysis methods and machine-learning models. The major challenges include limited and cultivar-specific datasets, environmental variability, laboratory-to-field transferability, insufficient external validation, high-dimensional data and the lack of standardized protocols. Future research should focus on compact and portable HSI systems, real-time inspection, artificial intelligence, multimodal sensing, transfer learning, standardized datasets and commercial-scale validation to support reliable and practical fruit quality assessment.

Abstract Integrated management of childhood illness (IMCI) guidelines have high sensitivity but low specificity for pneumonia diagnosis. Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled digital stethoscopes capable of analyzing lung sounds may improve IMCI diagnostic performance. We evaluated the performance of an AI algorithm trained to identify normal and adventitial lung sounds in children. Non-physician health workers recorded lung sounds from four chest positions using a digital stethoscope in under-five-year-old children with suspected pneumonia at community clinics in Bangladesh. A trained paediatrician listening panel classified chest position recordings as normal, abnormal (crackles and/or wheeze), or uninterpretable. The AI algorithm similarly classified chest position recordings except for the uninterpretable category. AI algorithm and listening panel comparisons were made at the child-level, and included chest positions considered interpretable, uninterpretable, and high- and low-confidence by the panel. Of 990 enrolled children, 867 (87%) had at least 3 interpretable chest position recordings by the panel and were analyzed. Compared to the panel, AI algorithm sensitivity and specificity for detecting abnormal sounds were 61.8% and 60.7% among all children, and 63.5% and 66.8% in IMCI pneumonia cases. Overall, the AI algorithm achieved moderate classification performance. Classification performance will benefit from further AI algorithm training to categorize recordings as uninterpretable.
